questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise and Peak of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Roman state went through two distinct periods of government. The Roman Republic existed from 509 BCE to 30 BCE. The Roman Empire then began in 30 BCE and lasted until 476 CE. While Rome technically had an empire during the Republican period, the term 'Roman Empire' specifically refers to the time period beginning with Augustus, when Rome was ruled by emperors instead of elected officials.
questions.question: What are the dates for the Roman Republic and the Roman Empire?
questions.answer: Roman Republic: 509 BCE-30 BCE; Roman Empire: 30 BCE-476 CE

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise and Peak of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: After defeating Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium, Octavian became sole ruler of Rome. The Senate gave him the title 'Augustus,' meaning 'most high.' He was made consul for life, 'Princeps' (first citizen), 'Imperator' (successful general), and 'Pontifex Maximus' (chief religious leader). Augustus reformed public morals by promoting family life, began the practice of declaring emperors gods, built and maintained the empire's infrastructure including roads, and extended citizenship to more provincials. He famously said he 'found Rome a city of bricks and left it a city of marble.'
questions.question: Augustus was given the title 'Imperator' by the Senate, which became the origin of the word 'emperor.'

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise and Peak of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Pax Romana, meaning Roman Peace, was a period of nearly 200 years during which Rome controlled the entire Mediterranean region and beyond. This complete control meant there was almost no warfare throughout the empire. More and more provincials were granted official Roman citizenship during this time. The Pax Romana began in 27 BCE with Augustus and ended in 180 CE with the death of Marcus Aurelius. During this golden age, Rome experienced unprecedented stability and prosperity.
questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the Pax Romana?
choices: A period of nearly 200 years of peace when Rome controlled the Mediterranean region
A military campaign that expanded Roman territory to its greatest extent
A treaty that ended the conflicts between Rome and Carthage
A religious movement that spread throughout the Roman Empire
questions.explanation: The Pax Romana was a period of approximately 200 years of peace and stability beginning in 27 BCE under Augustus and ending in 180 CE with Marcus Aurelius's death, during which Rome maintained complete control over the Mediterranean region.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Roman Emperors and Imperial Transformation
questions.lessonContent: When Augustus was made emperor, the Senate gave him several titles including 'Pontifex Maximus,' meaning 'chief religious leader.' This title originated with Augustus and remained tied to the Roman emperors. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire, the Bishops of Rome adopted this title to signify their religious authority. Today, the term 'pontiff' is still used to describe the pope, the leader of the Roman Catholic Church. The title demonstrates how Roman imperial traditions were adapted into religious institutions.
questions.question: What title given to Augustus is still used today to describe the pope?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Roman Emperors and Imperial Transformation
questions.lessonContent: Gaius Augustus Germanicus, who became Roman emperor in 37 CE, was nicknamed 'Caligula' by the Roman army during his childhood. The nickname 'Caligula' means 'little boots' and was given because he was dressed like a soldier while growing up among the troops. This childhood nickname remained with him throughout his life and became the name by which history remembers him. Caligula's reign began with two years of effective rule but ended catastrophically after a severe illness, as he became known for murdering family members and perceived enemies.
questions.question: Caligula earned his nickname 'Caligula,' meaning 'little boots,' from the Roman army when he was a child.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Roman Emperors and Imperial Transformation
questions.lessonTitle: The Emperor Who Divided the Empire
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Diocletian believe that dividing the empire into eastern and western administrative regions would strengthen it. In 285 CE, Diocletian became the first emperor to split the empire into two administrative realms, creating the Western (Roman) Empire and the Eastern (Byzantine) Empire. Constantine later moved the capital from Rome to Byzantium (renamed Constantinople), deepening the east-west split. The Western Empire officially ended in 476 CE when the last emperor Romulus Augustus was deposed, while the Eastern Byzantine Empire lasted until 1453 when conquered by the Ottoman Turks.
questions.question: Which emperor first divided the Roman Empire into Eastern and Western administrative regions?
questions.explanation: Diocletian first divided the empire into two administrative realms in 285 CE, creating the Western (Roman) and Eastern (Byzantine) empires. This was done to strengthen administrative efficiency, though it ultimately contributed to the permanent division of the empire.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Roman Emperors and Imperial Transformation
questions.lessonContent: After Emperor Nero's death in 68 CE, the Roman Empire experienced a brief period of civil war known as the Year of the Four Emperors in 69 CE. Galba became emperor after Nero, but was soon replaced by Otho when Galba was assassinated. Otho then ruled briefly before being overthrown by Vitellius, who had the support of the Rhine armies. Finally, Vespasian defeated Vitellius and established a new dynasty, bringing stability back to the empire.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Year of the Four Emperors?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall of Rome and Its Lasting Legacy
questions.lessonTitle: The Fall of the Western Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Diocletian had believed that dividing the empire for administrative purposes would strengthen the empire. He was wrong. Once Constantine set up Constantinople as a capital city, the east/west split deepened. The Western (Roman) Empire ended officially in 476 CE when the last emperor, Romulus Augustus, was deposed by a barbarian, Odoacer. The Eastern (Byzantine) Empire lasted until 1453 when the empire was conquered by the Ottoman Turks.
questions.question: In what year did the Western Roman Empire officially end?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall of Rome and Its Lasting Legacy
questions.lessonTitle: The Longevity of the Byzantine Empire
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Diocletian had believed that dividing the empire for administrative purposes would strengthen the empire. He was wrong. Once Constantine set up Constantinople as a capital city, the east/west split deepened. The Western (Roman) Empire ended officially in 476 CE when the last emperor, Romulus Augustus, was deposed by a barbarian, Odoacer. The Eastern (Byzantine) Empire lasted until 1453 when the empire was conquered by the Ottoman Turks.
questions.question: The Eastern (Byzantine) Empire lasted longer than the Western (Roman) Empire.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall of Rome and Its Lasting Legacy
questions.lessonContent: Justinian was a powerful emperor of the Eastern (Byzantine) empire headquartered at Constantinople. He married Theodora, an intelligent courtesan. Justinian managed to reunite the Eastern and Western empires for a time, but this did not last. He rewrote Roman law (Corpus Juris Civilis, or the Justinian Code), which is still the basis for civil law in several countries. The Plague of Justinian (541-542 CE) was a bubonic plague that severely hurt the Byzantine empire, but Emperor Justinian became sick and recovered.
questions.question: Which of the following was an accomplishment of Emperor Justinian?
choices: He divided the empire into Eastern and Western administrative regions
He converted to Christianity and granted religious toleration through the Edict of Milan
He established Constantinople as the new capital of the Roman Empire
He rewrote Roman law in the Corpus Juris Civilis, which became the basis for civil law in several countries
questions.explanation: Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis (Justinian Code) encapsulated over 1000 years of Roman law and remains the basis for civil law in many parts of Europe today.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall of Rome and Its Lasting Legacy
questions.lessonTitle: The Christianization of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The relationship between Christianity and the Roman Empire evolved dramatically over several centuries. Under Emperor Nero in 64 CE, Christians were blamed for the Great Fire of Rome and persecuted as a new religious group. Nearly 250 years later, Emperor Constantine legalized Christianity through the Edict of Milan in 313 CE, granting religious toleration throughout the empire. Finally, Constantine himself converted to Christianity on his deathbed in 337 CE, and subsequent Roman emperors also became Christians, transforming Christianity from a persecuted sect to the favored religion of the Roman Empire.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Christianization of the Roman Empire?

results.file: How we built our multi-agent research system _ Anthropic.pdf

questions.lessonTitle: What Defines a Multi-Agent Research System
questions.lessonContent: A multi-agent research system consists of multiple agents, defined as LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop, working together to accomplish complex tasks. In Anthropic's Research feature, the system uses an agent that plans a research process based on user queries and then uses tools to create parallel agents that search for information simultaneously. The lead agent analyzes queries, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously. This architecture enables the system to handle open-ended research problems that are inherently dynamic and path-dependent, where the required steps cannot be predicted in advance.
questions.question: What is the definition of a multi-agent system according to the source content?
questions.answer: A multi-agent system consists of multiple agents (LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop) working together

questions.lessonTitle: Multi-Agent Systems Outperform Single-Agent Systems on Research Tasks
questions.lessonContent: Internal evaluations at Anthropic show that multi-agent research systems excel especially for breadth-first queries involving pursuing multiple independent directions simultaneously. The evaluation tested a multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents against a single-agent Claude Opus 4 system. When asked to identify all the board members of companies in the Information Technology S&P 500, the multi-agent system succeeded by decomposing the task into subagent searches while the single-agent system failed with slow, sequential searches. The performance improvement was measured as a 90.2% gain on their internal research evaluation.
questions.question: A multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed a single-agent Claude Opus 4 system by 90.2% on the internal research evaluation.

questions.lessonTitle: Token Usage in Multi-Agent Research Systems
questions.lessonContent: Analysis of the BrowseComp evaluation, which tests browsing agents' ability to locate hard-to-find information, revealed three factors explaining 95% of performance variance. Token usage alone explained 80% of the variance, with the number of tool calls and model choice as the other explanatory factors. Multi-agent architectures distribute work across agents with separate context windows, adding capacity for parallel reasoning. In practice, agents typically use about 4× more tokens than standard chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats. These systems require tasks where the value is high enough to justify the increased token consumption.
questions.question: Based on the performance analysis, what percentage of variance in the BrowseComp evaluation was explained by token usage alone?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance in the BrowseComp evaluation, making this the correct answer.

questions.lessonContent: The multi-agent research system follows a coordinated workflow where the Lead Agent first analyzes the user's query and develops a strategic plan for research. Once the plan is established, the Lead Agent Spawns Parallel Subagents to explore different aspects of the topic simultaneously. Each subagent then independently performs searches, evaluates the results using interleaved thinking, and returns findings. This sequential process allows the system to efficiently decompose complex research questions into parallel investigations before synthesizing the final results.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the multi-agent research system workflow?

questions.moduleTitle: Prompt Engineering, Tool Design, and Evaluation Strategies
questions.lessonContent: We found that the Claude 4 models can be excellent prompt engineers. When given a prompt and a failure mode, they are able to diagnose why the agent is failing and suggest improvements. We even created a tool-testing agent—when given a flawed MCP tool, it attempts to use the tool and then rewrites the tool description to avoid failures. By testing the tool dozens of times, this agent found key nuances and bugs. This process for improving tool ergonomics resulted in a 40% decrease in task completion time for future agents using the new description, because they were able to avoid most mistakes.
questions.question: What percentage decrease in task completion time resulted from the tool-testing agent's improved tool descriptions?

questions.moduleTitle: Prompt Engineering, Tool Design, and Evaluation Strategies
questions.lessonContent: LLM-as-judge evaluation scales when done well. Research outputs are difficult to evaluate programmatically since they are free-form text and rarely have a single correct answer. LLMs are a natural fit for grading outputs. We used an LLM judge that evaluated each output against criteria in a rubric: factual accuracy (do claims match sources?), citation accuracy (do the cited sources match the claims?), completeness (are all requested aspects covered?), source quality (did it use primary sources over lower-quality secondary sources?), and tool efficiency (did it use the right tools a reasonable number of times?). We experimented with multiple judges to evaluate each component, but found that a single LLM call with a single prompt outputting scores from 0.0-1.0 and a pass-fail grade was the most consistent and aligned with human judgements.
questions.question: LLM-as-judge evaluation of research outputs considers factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, and tool efficiency.

questions.moduleTitle: Prompt Engineering, Tool Design, and Evaluation Strategies
questions.lessonContent: Tool design and selection are critical. Agent-tool interfaces are as critical as human-computer interfaces. Using the right tool is efficient—often, it’s strictly necessary. For instance, an agent searching the web for context that only exists in Slack is doomed from the start. With MCP servers that give the model access to external tools, this problem compounds, as agents encounter unseen tools with descriptions of wildly varying quality. We gave our agents explicit heuristics: for example, examine all available tools first, match tool usage to user intent, search the web for broad external exploration, or prefer specialized tools over generic ones. Bad tool descriptions can send agents down completely wrong paths, so each tool needs a distinct purpose and a clear description.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the explicit heuristics Anthropic gave their agents for tool selection?
choices: Examine all available tools first before selecting
Match tool usage to user intent
Prefer generic tools over specialized ones for broader coverage
Search the web for broad external exploration
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 'Prefer generic tools over specialized ones for broader coverage' because the source explicitly states the heuristic is to 'prefer specialized tools over generic ones', not the reverse.

questions.lessonTitle: Rainbow Deployments for Stateful Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: Agent systems are highly stateful webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously. This means that whenever updates are deployed, agents might be anywhere in their process. Engineers cannot update every agent to the new version at the same time, as well-meaning code changes could break existing agents mid-task. Instead, Anthropic uses rainbow deployments to avoid disrupting running agents by gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously.
questions.question: What deployment strategy does Anthropic use to prevent code changes from breaking existing agents mid-process?

questions.lessonTitle: Synchronous Execution Limitations in Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: Currently, lead agents execute subagents synchronously, waiting for each set of subagents to complete before proceeding. This simplifies coordination but creates bottlenecks in the information flow between agents. The lead agent cannot steer subagents in real-time, subagents cannot coordinate with each other, and the entire system can be blocked while waiting for a single subagent to finish searching. Asynchronous execution would enable additional parallelism where agents work concurrently and create new subagents when needed.
questions.question: In the current Anthropic Research system architecture, the lead agent executes subagents synchronously, which creates bottlenecks and prevents subagents from coordinating with each other in real-time.

questions.lessonTitle: Evaluating Agents That Modify Persistent State
questions.lessonContent: Evaluating agents that modify persistent state across multi-turn conversations presents unique challenges unlike read-only research tasks. Each action can change the environment for subsequent steps, creating dependencies that traditional evaluation methods struggle to handle. Anthropic found success focusing on end-state evaluation rather than turn-by-turn analysis. Instead of judging whether the agent followed a specific process, they evaluate whether it achieved the correct final state. For complex workflows, evaluation breaks into discrete checkpoints where specific state changes should have occurred.
questions.question: What evaluation approach does Anthropic use for agents that modify persistent state across multiple turns?
choices: Path validation - verifying that agents took the exact correct route to reach the goal
End-state evaluation - evaluating whether the agent achieved the correct final state rather than judging the process
Output-only assessment - only checking the final output without considering state changes
Turn-by-turn analysis - checking if the agent followed specific prescribed steps at each stage
questions.explanation: For agents that mutate state over many turns, end-state evaluation focuses on whether the correct final state was achieved rather than requiring the agent to follow a specific prescribed process. This approach acknowledges that agents may find alternative paths to the same goal.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Foundation, Architecture, and Continued Pretraining
questions.lessonContent: The Composer 2 model was built by extending Kimi K2.5, a 1.04 trillion parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 32 billion active parameters. The selection of this base model was guided by internal evaluations measuring codebase perplexity, coding knowledge through FreshBench, and state tracking capabilities. FreshBench is a question-answer benchmark adversarially constructed against previous Composer models that identifies scenarios where models had to read library source code or perform web searches to solve coding tasks. Kimi K2.5 achieved 83.2% on FreshBench, outperforming both DeepSeek V3.2 (68.9%) and GLM-5 (79.2%). State tracking was measured using an internal benchmark similar to LoCoDiff, which tests the model's ability to understand file states after many diffs, an important capability for long-term memory in coding agents.
questions.question: What is the name of the base model used for Composer 2?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Foundation, Architecture, and Continued Pretraining
questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage for Composer 2 was divided into three distinct phases to improve the model's base knowledge in the domain of coding. The first and most compute-intensive phase used a 32k token sequence length, representing the bulk of the training computation. This was followed by a shorter long-context extension phase that expanded the model's context window to 256k tokens. Finally, a short supervised fine-tuning phase was conducted on targeted coding tasks. Throughout this training, the evaluation loss on the internal codebase was measured and found to decrease log-linearly over the course of the training run. This multi-phase approach builds on recent research showing that progressively filtering towards higher quality data yields improved downstream performance.
questions.question: The 32k token sequence length phase represents the bulk of the compute budget in Composer 2's continued pretraining.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Foundation, Architecture, and Continued Pretraining
questions.lessonContent: To serve the Composer 2 model faster in production, additional Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) layers were trained for use with speculative decoding. These MTP layers were initialized from scratch rather than being copied from existing weights. They were trained on the same data mix as the main model using self-distillation, which teaches the model to predict the exact logit distribution of the main LM head at each position. To speed up convergence, the MTP layers were trained atop a checkpoint cut from the middle of the continued pretraining run rather than the initial or final checkpoint. Importantly, during the final two phases of continued pretraining (the long-context extension to 256k tokens and the SFT phase), the MTP layers were included and trained jointly with the rest of the model.
questions.question: How were the Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) layers initialized for Composer 2 training?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that MTP layers were initialized from scratch and trained on the same data mix using self-distillation to predict the exact logit distribution of the main LM head at each position.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Foundation, Architecture, and Continued Pretraining
questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage in Composer 2 training is divided into three distinct phases to specialize the model on coding knowledge and capabilities. First, the bulk of compute is spent at 32k token sequence length to build foundational coding knowledge. This is followed by a shorter long-context extension phase that extends the model's context window to 256k sequence length. Finally, a short SFT phase on targeted coding tasks prepares the model for downstream applications. The correct order of these phases determines the effectiveness of the final coding agent.
questions.question: What is the correct order of phases in Composer 2's continued pretraining stage?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Reinforcement Learning and Agent Behavior
questions.lessonTitle: Single-Epoch Training Regime in Composer 2's RL Pipeline
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2's reinforcement learning pipeline operates in a distinct training regime called the single-epoch regime. In this approach, the same prompt is never trained on twice throughout the entire reinforcement learning process. Each problem is sampled from the distribution, multiple rollouts are simulated with different solutions, and then the model weights are updated based on solution quality. This design ensures that the model sees each training example exactly one time, preventing overfitting to specific problem instances. The single-epoch regime is a key characteristic of how Composer 2 learns from its large set of coding tasks.
questions.question: In which training regime does Composer 2 operate where the same prompt is never trained on twice?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Reinforcement Learning and Agent Behavior
questions.lessonTitle: Removal of Length Standardization from GRPO
questions.lessonContent: In Composer 2's reinforcement learning training, the policy gradient algorithm follows the approach from Dr. GRPO research. A crucial finding in this work was that removing the length standardization term from GRPO eliminates a length bias in the gradient estimation. The length standardization term, when present, artificially adjusts advantages based on response length, which can skew the learning signal. By removing this term, the model receives unbiased gradients that more accurately reflect true solution quality rather than length-based artifacts. This modification helps maintain the integrity of the learning process for coding tasks of varying complexity.
questions.question: In Composer 2's RL training, removing the length standardization term from GRPO prevents the introduction of length bias in the gradients.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Reinforcement Learning and Agent Behavior
questions.lessonTitle: Nonlinear Length Penalty Formula in Composer 2
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 implements a sophisticated reward mechanism to shape agent behavior through a concave down and increasing nonlinear length penalty. This penalty is designed to incentivize the model to produce solutions quickly on easy requests while allowing it to think longer on hard requests. The formula uses two hyperparameters called k and q which define the curvature of the penalty curve. The input x is a weighted combination of thinking tokens, tool calling tokens, tool output tokens, final message tokens, number of tool calls, and number of turns of a rollout. This nonlinear approach reflects that on easy tasks achievable with only a few tool calls, every additional bit of effort is felt more acutely than in long-horizon tasks where the agent might iterate for hundreds of tool calls.
questions.question: What are the two hyperparameters that define the curvature of the nonlinear length penalty used to incentivize efficient behavior in Composer 2?
questions.explanation: The formula Clength{k,q}(x) = ((1 + kx)^(1-q) - 1) / (k(1-q)) explicitly uses k and q as the hyperparameters which define the curvature of the penalty curve.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Reinforcement Learning and Agent Behavior
questions.lessonContent: In Composer 2's reinforcement learning training, the process begins by sampling a problem and generating multiple rollouts from the agent. After rollouts are collected, the next step involves Compute Rewards, where each rollout receives a reward based on the code's correctness, succinctness, and conformance to software engineering principles. Following reward computation, the pipeline proceeds to Calculate Advantages, which involves comparing the performance of different rollouts to determine which actions contributed positively to the outcome. Finally, the model performs Update Weights using the calculated advantages to improve the policy through gradient-based optimization.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in Composer 2's RL training optimization process?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Real-World Evaluation, Benchmarks, and Infrastructure
questions.lessonContent: CursorBench represents a significant advancement in evaluating coding agents by using tasks derived from actual coding sessions rather than curated public repositories. The structural differences between CursorBench and public evaluation sets are substantial: CursorBench tasks require substantially more extensive code modifications, with a median of 181 lines changed compared to just 7-10 lines for SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. Additionally, CursorBench prompts are more under-specified, featuring a median description length of only 390 characters versus 1,185-3,055 characters for public benchmarks. This combination of broad execution scope and high intent ambiguity accurately reflects the intrinsic difficulty of real-world software engineering.
questions.question: What is the median number of lines changed in CursorBench tasks?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Real-World Evaluation, Benchmarks, and Infrastructure
questions.lessonContent: Beyond measuring functional correctness on CursorBench, the evaluation framework also incorporates targeted evaluations covering other critical aspects of coding agent quality and behavior. These supplementary evaluations include an intent evaluation, which assesses how the model handles ambiguous prompts; an instruction-following evaluation, which measures how well the model follows system prompts, user prompts, rules, and skills; and an eager editing evaluation, which tests how the model responds to questions where it should avoid editing code. Additional evaluations judge the quality of code and comments, as well as how the model handles mid-rollout interruptions and user feedback. These evaluations are developed by identifying important dimensions of agent behavior, selecting data points that elicit them, and writing rubrics to measure performance.
questions.question: CursorBench evaluates functional correctness along with code quality, execution efficiency, and interactive agent behavior in realistic settings.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Real-World Evaluation, Benchmarks, and Infrastructure
questions.lessonTitle: Precision Formats Used in Composer 2 Training
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 training employs specific low-precision formats to optimize the Mixture-of-Experts layer performance. The training recipe uses both MXFP8 and NVFP4 precision formats, exclusively targeting NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs for block-scaled tensor-core matrix multiplications. For the MoE forward pass, a novel variant of NVFP4 is used where values are quantized from BF16 into FP4E2M1 using FP8E4M3 per-block scales (block size = 16) and FP32 per-token scales. For the MoE backward pass, the standard MXFP8 format is used with FP8E4M3 values and FP8E8M0 scales per 32-element block. The asymmetry in RL training allows this approach: the forward pass requires numerical matching between trainer and inference for stability (using NVFP4), while the backward pass runs only on the training cluster and can afford higher precision.
questions.question: Which precision formats are used in Composer 2 training for the MoE layer?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that Composer 2 training uses both MXFP8 and NVFP4 precision formats for the Mixture-of-Experts layer, targeting NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs for block-scaled tensor-core matrix multiplications.

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. You can place CLAUDE.md files in several locations: the root of your repo where you run claude from (the most common usage), any parent of the directory where you run claude (useful for monorepos), any child of the directory where you run claude (Claude pulls these in on demand when working with files in child directories), and your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md which applies to all Claude sessions. When running the /init command, Claude will automatically generate a CLAUDE.md for you.
questions.question: In which directory should you place a CLAUDE.md file if you want it to apply to all Claude sessions across all projects?

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code requests permission for actions that might modify your system, designed with a deliberately conservative approach to prioritize safety. You can customize the allowlist to permit additional tools that you know are safe. There are four ways to manage allowed tools: select "Always allow" when prompted during a session, use the /permissions command after starting Claude Code to add or remove tools, manually edit your .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json (recommend checking the former into source control to share with your team), and use the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions.
questions.question: The /permissions command can be used to add or remove tools from the allowlist after starting Claude Code.

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code functions as both an MCP server and client, able to connect to any number of MCP servers to access their tools. MCP servers can be configured in three ways: in project config (available when running Claude Code in that directory), in global config (available in all projects), and in a checked-in .mcp.json file which makes tools available to anyone working in your codebase. When working with MCP, launching Claude with the --mcp-debug flag helps identify configuration issues.
questions.question: What are the three ways to configure MCP servers in Claude Code?
choices: Project config, global config, and .mcp.json file
Init command, permissions command, and config command
Settings.json, environment variables, and CLI flags
Bash commands, REST APIs, and Claude commands
questions.explanation: MCP servers can be configured in project config (available in that directory), global config (available in all projects), or via a checked-in .mcp.json file (available to anyone working in the codebase).

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonTitle: Setting Up Your Claude Code Environment
questions.lessonContent: When customizing Claude Code, the first step is to create a CLAUDE.md file in your repository root or home folder. This file automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation, making it ideal for documenting bash commands, code style guidelines, and developer environment setup. After creating your CLAUDE.md files, you should tune them by adding content manually or using the # key to incorporate instructions while coding. Finally, you need to configure allowed tools by selecting 'Always allow' when prompted, using the /permissions command, or manually editing your settings.json file.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in customizing your Claude Code environment?

questions.lessonTitle: Thinking Budget Keywords in Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: When asking Claude to plan solutions, you can trigger extended thinking mode by using specific phrases. These phrases are mapped directly to increasing levels of thinking budget in the system. The lowest level uses the word 'think', followed by 'think hard', then 'think harder', and finally 'ultrathink' at the highest level. Each progressive keyword allocates more thinking budget for Claude to evaluate alternatives more thoroughly during problem-solving.
questions.question: What is the correct order of thinking budget keywords from lowest to highest in Claude Code?
questions.answer: think, think hard, think harder, ultrathink

questions.lessonTitle: Test-Driven Development Workflow in Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code supports a test-driven development workflow where tests are written before implementation code. In this workflow, you ask Claude to write tests based on expected input/output pairs and explicitly tell it not to create any mock implementations, even for functionality that doesn't exist yet. Then you tell Claude to run the tests and confirm they fail. Only after confirming test failures do you ask Claude to write code that passes the tests, instructing it not to modify the tests. Claude will iterate through writing code, running tests, and adjusting until all tests pass.
questions.question: In the test-driven development workflow for Claude Code, you should ask Claude to write implementation code only after confirming that the tests fail.

questions.lessonTitle: Methods for Providing Visual Targets to Claude
questions.lessonContent: When working with Claude Code on visual tasks, you can provide visual targets through multiple methods. You can give Claude a way to take browser screenshots using tools like the Puppeteer MCP server or iOS simulator MCP server, or manually copy and paste screenshots. Additionally, you can copy and paste images directly, drag and drop images into the prompt input, or provide file paths for images. This enables Claude to implement designs in code, take screenshots of results, and iterate until its output matches the visual mock.
questions.question: Which of the following methods can you use to provide visual targets to Claude Code for UI development?
choices: Only provide file paths to image directories
Only take screenshots using the Puppeteer MCP server
Only copy and paste images from the clipboard
Paste screenshots, drag and drop images, or provide image file paths
questions.explanation: Claude Code accepts visual targets through multiple methods: pasting screenshots, dragging and dropping images directly into the prompt input, and providing file paths for images. This flexibility allows for various workflows when working with visual mocks for UI development.

questions.lessonContent: In the test-driven development (TDD) workflow, you first ask Claude to write tests based on expected input/output pairs. Next, you tell Claude to run the tests and confirm they fail, explicitly instructing it not to write any implementation code at this stage. Finally, when you're satisfied with the tests, you ask Claude to commit them before moving on to implementation.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the test-driven development workflow?

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code includes headless mode for non-interactive contexts like CI, pre-commit hooks, build scripts, and automation. To enable headless mode, you use the -p flag followed by your prompt. For streaming JSON output, you use the --output-format stream-json flag. It's important to note that headless mode does not persist between sessions, meaning you have to trigger it each time you need to run a session. This mode is particularly useful for automating infrastructure tasks and running Claude in CI/CD pipelines.
questions.question: What flag do you use to enable headless mode in Claude Code?

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code headless mode allows automation in non-interactive contexts such as CI pipelines and pre-commit hooks. When using headless mode, the session operates without user interaction. However, since each invocation starts a new session, you must trigger headless mode each time you want to run it.
questions.question: Headless mode in Claude Code persists between sessions, allowing you to continue a previous session without re-enabling it.

questions.lessonContent: Beyond standalone usage, powerful applications involve running multiple Claude instances in parallel. One approach is having one Claude write code while another reviews or tests it in separate terminals. Another technique is creating multiple git checkouts in separate folders, opening each folder in separate terminal tabs, and starting Claude in each folder with different tasks. A lighter-weight alternative uses git worktrees, which allow checking out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories while sharing the same Git history.
questions.question: Which of the following is a recommended approach for running multiple Claude sessions simultaneously on different parts of your project?
choices: Use git worktrees to check out multiple branches into separate directories
Use multiple git checkouts in separate folders
Have one Claude write code while another reviews in the same terminal
Use the --persist flag to maintain multiple sessions
questions.explanation: Git worktrees allow you to check out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories, with each worktree having its own working directory with isolated files while sharing the same Git history and reflog.

questions.lessonTitle: Git Worktrees for Parallel Claude Sessions
questions.lessonContent: The git worktrees workflow enables running multiple Claude sessions simultaneously on different parts of your project. First, you create a git worktree using 'git worktree add ../project-feature-a feature-a'. Then, you launch Claude in each worktree by navigating to the directory and running 'claude'. Finally, you assign independent tasks to each Claude instance, allowing them to work on separate features without merge conflicts.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the git worktrees workflow for running multiple Claude sessions in parallel?

questions.lessonContent: Text embeddings provide a numerical representation that measures the similarity or relatedness between text queries. This mathematical representation allows computers to understand semantic relationships between different pieces of text. Embeddings are fundamental to many natural language processing applications because they convert textual information into dense vector representations. These vector representations capture semantic meaning rather than just literal word matches. The technology enables machines to perform sophisticated tasks like finding related documents or grouping similar content together.
questions.question: What do text embeddings provide a measure of?
questions.answer: similarity or relatedness of given text queries

questions.lessonContent: The M2-BERT retrieval models available through Together Embeddings support extremely long document processing without requiring chunking. These state-of-the-art long context models can handle context lengths of 2k, 8k, and 32k tokens respectively. This capability allows users to generate embeddings for lengthy documents while preserving meaningful contextual information. The ability to process up to 32k context length means users can embed entire long-form documents in a single API call. This represents a significant advantage over platforms that require splitting longer documents into multiple shorter chunks.
questions.question: The M2-BERT retrieval models from Together Embeddings support context lengths up to 32k tokens.

questions.lessonContent: Together Embeddings offers pricing that is significantly more competitive compared to other popular embedding platforms. The pricing advantage combines with the model's performance capabilities to provide value. Users can access state-of-the-art embedding models at a fraction of typical industry costs.
questions.question: Which pricing advantage does Together Embeddings offer compared to other platforms?

questions.lessonContent: In the data visualization example using Together Embeddings, the process involves several key steps. First, you generate embeddings using the Together API with the specified model. Next, you transform these high-dimensional embedding vectors using tSNE to reduce them to 2D for visualization. Finally, you plot the transformed embeddings to visualize the data. This sequential process allows you to take raw text data, convert it to embeddings, reduce the dimensionality, and create a visual representation of the data clusters.

questions.lessonContent: Text embeddings provide a measure of similarity or relatedness between text queries, making them essential for various applications. Embeddings are particularly useful for clustering similar documents together, performing semantic search to find related content, and classifying text into predefined categories. Additionally, embeddings enable retrieval augmented generation (RAG), which addresses a key limitation of generative AI models: their lack of knowledge from unseen data. RAG works by finding relevant information from a knowledge base through embeddings and providing that information to a generative model.

results.file: How does image compression work_ _ Lee Robinson.pdf

questions.moduleTitle: Introduction to Images and Compression Fundamentals
questions.lessonTitle: Understanding Digital Images and Pixel Values
questions.lessonContent: Images look smooth and continuous, but zooming in reveals they are made of tiny colored squares called pixels. Each pixel contains three numbers representing how much red, green, and blue to mix together to create its color. Each of these three color values ranges from 0, indicating no presence of that color, to 255, representing maximum intensity of that color. For example, the orange color rgb(255, 147, 41) has red at maximum (255), green at 147, and blue at 41. This RGB system is the foundation of how digital images represent color on computers.
questions.question: What is the range of possible values for each of the red, green, and blue components in a pixel?

questions.moduleTitle: Introduction to Images and Compression Fundamentals
questions.lessonContent: A standard HD screenshot has dimensions of 1920 × 1080 pixels, which equals over 2 million total pixels. Since each pixel requires 3 bytes of storage (one byte each for red, green, and blue), the math works out to over 6 million bytes for a single image. Specifically, 1,920 × 1,080 equals 2,073,600 pixels, and multiplying by 3 bytes gives 6,220,800 bytes, which is approximately 6.2 megabytes. This large file size demonstrates why compression is essential for storing and transmitting images efficiently.
questions.question: An HD screenshot with dimensions 1920 × 1080 pixels and 3 bytes per pixel results in approximately a 6.2 MB file size.

questions.moduleTitle: Introduction to Images and Compression Fundamentals
questions.lessonTitle: The Two Fundamental Approaches to Image Compression
questions.lessonContent: Image compression uses two distinct approaches to reduce file sizes. The first approach, called lossy compression, throws away parts of the data that humans won't notice, trading some quality for much smaller file sizes. The second approach, called lossless compression, preserves every single pixel perfectly while still achieving file size reduction through clever storage methods. Lossy compression (used by JPEG) exploits how human vision works, as our eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together. Lossless compression (used by PNG) keeps all original data intact, which is essential for images like screenshots with text or graphics requiring sharp edges.
questions.question: Which of the following describes the two main approaches to image compression?
choices: All image formats use both lossy and lossless compression simultaneously
Compression is unnecessary for images smaller than 1 megabyte
Lossy compression throws away data humans won't notice, while lossless compression keeps every pixel perfectly
JPEG uses only lossless compression to preserve all image details
questions.explanation: The correct answer accurately describes the two fundamental compression approaches: lossy compression (like JPEG) discards imperceptible data, while lossless compression (like PNG) preserves every pixel exactly. The other options are incorrect because JPEG specifically uses lossy compression, not all formats combine both approaches, and compression benefits images of all sizes.

questions.moduleTitle: Introduction to Images and Compression Fundamentals
questions.lessonTitle: Introduction to Images and Compression Fundamentals
questions.lessonContent: PNG combines three essential tricks in sequence to achieve lossless compression. First, Filtering stores differences between pixels rather than absolute values, making the data easier to compress. Second, LZ77 Pattern Finding replaces repeated patterns with back-references, eliminating redundant information. Third, Huffman Encoding gives common values shorter binary codes while assigning longer codes to rare values. Finally, the result gets wrapped in PNG format with headers and checksums.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the PNG lossless compression pipeline?

questions.lessonTitle: Human Visual Perception in JPEG Compression
questions.lessonContent: Lossy compression used by JPEG exploits how human vision works. Your eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together. You notice a blurry edge, but you won't notice if colors are slightly off. JPEG takes advantage of this by converting pixels from RGB to a different format that separates brightness from color, and reduces color resolution since your eyes won't notice. This allows JPEG to throw away color data that humans cannot perceive while preserving the brightness information.
questions.question: What aspect of human vision does JPEG primarily exploit to achieve compression?
questions.answer: The eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together

questions.lessonContent: Lossy compression achieves its small file sizes by actually throwing away data. Unlike lossless methods that preserve every pixel, lossy compression permanently removes information from the original file. When you compress an image using JPEG's lossy approach, you cannot get the original pixels back - the data is gone forever. The tradeoff is that you achieve 10-20x smaller files with minimal visible difference at high quality settings, but the compression is irreversible.
questions.question: With lossy compression like JPEG, you can recover the exact original pixels by decompressing the file.

questions.lessonContent: JPEG uses a specific technique to process image data for compression. First, it converts pixels from RGB to a format separating brightness from color. It also reduces color resolution since human eyes are less sensitive to color details. Then, JPEG divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components. Low frequencies represent smooth gradients in photographs, while high frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges. Since photographs are mostly smooth gradients, most information ends up in just a few low-frequency components, allowing JPEG to throw away high-frequency details.
questions.question: What block size does JPEG use when transforming image data into frequency components?
questions.explanation: JPEG divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components representing smooth gradients (low frequency) and fine details (high frequency).

questions.lessonContent: PNG uses a technique called filtering or prediction to compress image data. Instead of storing the raw pixel values, PNG stores how much each pixel differs from its neighbor. PNG supports four prediction methods: Sub predicts from the left neighbor (best for horizontal gradients), Up predicts from the pixel above (best for vertical gradients), Average predicts from the average of left and above, and Paeth intelligently picks between left, above, or diagonal. PNG encoders try each method per row and select the one that achieves the best compression for that particular row of data.
questions.question: Which PNG prediction method is described as intelligently picking between left, above, or diagonal?

questions.lessonContent: Lossless compression (used by PNG) preserves every single pixel while still shrinking the file size. Unlike lossy compression which throws away data humans won't notice, lossless compression uses clever techniques to represent the same information more efficiently. For a photograph, a 6.2 MB image can become around 2.1 MB using lossless compression—3x smaller with zero quality loss. Screenshots with large solid color regions can achieve even more impressive compression ratios of 10-50x.
questions.question: Lossless compression maintains all original pixel data without any loss of quality.

questions.lessonContent: After filtering and pattern-finding with LZ77, some values appear more frequently than others in the data. Huffman coding gives these common values shorter binary codes to achieve compression. For example, if the value 0 appears 60% of the time, it might get just 1 bit (0). Values appearing 25% of the time might get 2 bits (10), while rare values appearing only 5% of the time get longer 3-bit codes (111). This same principle underlies Morse code, where the common letter 'E' uses just one dot (•) while rare letters use longer sequences.
questions.question: According to the example in the content, which value receives the shortest code in Huffman coding?
questions.explanation: The value 0, which appears most frequently (60% of the time), receives the shortest 1-bit code in Huffman coding, demonstrating how common values get shorter binary representations.

questions.lessonContent: A PNG file is organized into sequential chunks, each serving a specific purpose. The PNG Signature (89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A) appears first and identifies the file as PNG. Following the signature, the IHDR Chunk (Image Header) must appear as the first chunk, containing critical metadata like width, height, bit depth, and color type. The actual compressed image data is stored in subsequent IDAT Chunks, which contain the filtered and compressed pixel data. The IEND Chunk marks the end of the file.
questions.question: What is the correct order of chunks when constructing a basic PNG file?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise and Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Transition from Roman Republic to Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: There were two periods of Roman government. The Roman Republic lasted from 509 BCE to 30 BCE, while the Roman Empire lasted from 30 BCE to 476 CE. Although Rome technically had an empire under the Roman Republic, the term "Roman Empire" specifically refers to the time period beginning with Augustus when Rome was ruled by emperors. Octavian became the sole ruler of Rome after his forces defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium. The Senate then gave Octavian the name "Augustus," which means "most high."
questions.question: What are the dates for the Roman Republic and the Roman Empire?
questions.answer: Roman Republic: 509 BCE-30 BCE; Roman Empire: 30 BCE-476 CE

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise and Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Concept of Primus Inter Pares
questions.lessonContent: The Latin phrase "primus inter pares" means "first among equals." Augustus and later emperors tried to maintain the façade that they were elected officials rather than dictators. Being "first among equals" gave the illusion that an emperor was the most prestigious and important member of the Roman Senate, but that each senator was simultaneously equally important. In reality, the Roman emperors ruled with little input from anyone else. The Senate awarded Augustus the titles of "Princeps" (first citizen), "Imperator" (successful general), and "Pontifex Maximus" (chief religious leader).
questions.question: Primus inter pares was a phrase used to describe how Augustus and later emperors presented themselves as equal to senators while actually holding supreme power.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise and Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Augustus attempted to reform public morals by promoting family life, though this was largely unsuccessful. He began the practice of declaring emperors gods and of picking their own successors. Augustus built and maintained the empire's infrastructure, including roads, and encouraged the growth of business. He established fire and police departments for Rome and created a strong money system. Augustus extended citizenship to more and more provincials and famously said he "found Rome a city of bricks and left it a city of marble." Jesus, the founder of Christianity, was born in the Roman province of Judea during the reign of Augustus.
questions.question: Which of these actions did Augustus perform?
choices: He established fire and police departments for Rome
He built and maintained the empire's infrastructure
He established the first Roman Senate
questions.explanation: The Senate existed during the Roman Republic, long before Augustus came to power. Therefore, Augustus did not establish the first Roman Senate - he found it already existing. The other three options are all accomplishments of Augustus: he built infrastructure, established fire and police departments, and extended citizenship to provincials.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise and Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Rise and Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Octavian's rise to power followed a precise sequence of events. After defeating Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium, Octavian became the sole ruler of Rome. The Senate then honored him with the name 'Augustus,' meaning 'most high.' Finally, in 23 BCE, Augustus was made consul for life by the Senate, cementing his political authority.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in Octavian's rise to become Augustus and establish the Roman Empire?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Peak, Division, and Fall of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Pax Romana: Duration and Extent
questions.lessonContent: The Pax Romana, or Roman Peace, was a period of relative peace and stability in the Roman Empire. Rome controlled the entire Mediterranean region and beyond, and this complete control meant almost no warfare. This peace lasted nearly 200 years, from 27 BCE until 180 CE, when the reign of Marcus Aurelius ended. During this time, more and more provincials were granted official Roman citizenship, and the empire reached its greatest territorial extent under Emperor Trajan.
questions.question: How long did the Pax Romana last?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Peak, Division, and Fall of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Diocletian believed that dividing the empire for administrative purposes would strengthen the empire. In 285 CE, he divided the empire into two administrative realms (east and west), creating the Western (Roman) Empire and the Eastern (Byzantine) Empire. This was the first step in the creation of what would become two separate empires. Once Constantine set up Constantinople as a capital city, the east/west split deepened further.
questions.question: Emperor Diocletian divided the empire into two administrative realms (east and west) in 285 CE to strengthen it for administrative purposes.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Peak, Division, and Fall of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: Reasons for the Fall of the Western Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Western Roman Empire fell due to multiple interconnected factors. Economically, there was a gap between rich and poor, and impoverished workers became tied to the land as coloni. Militarily, armies made and unmade emperors, and reliance on barbarian troops who were not ultimately loyal to Rome proved problematic. Politically, there was no orderly succession, with murders, forced suicides, and civil wars frequently accompanying transitions between emperors. Additionally, democracy did not exist in reality, and citizens lost their tie (voting rights) to the state as part of the decline in patriotism. Socially, population decline from hunger, plagues, and war, combined with a decline in intellectual culture, weakened the empire.
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT mentioned as a reason for the fall of the Western Roman Empire?
choices: Expansion of democratic voting rights to all citizens
Economic gap between rich and poor
questions.explanation: The content mentions economic reasons (gap between rich and poor), military reasons (barbarian troops not loyal to Rome), political reasons (no orderly succession with murders and civil wars), and social reasons (population decline, decline in intellectual culture). However, the source explicitly states that democracy did not exist in reality and that citizens lost their voting rights as part of the decline in patriotism. There was no 'expansion of democratic voting rights' mentioned—the source discusses the LOSS of voting rights, not their expansion to all citizens.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Peak, Division, and Fall of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Division and Fall of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The process of the Roman Empire's division and eventual fall involved several critical steps. Emperor Diocletian divided the empire into two administrative realms in 285 CE as the first step in what would become a permanent split. Later, Constantine moved the capital from Rome to Byzantium, renaming it Constantinople, which shifted the political center eastward. Ultimately, the Western Roman Empire ended in 476 CE when the last emperor, Romulus Augustus, was deposed by the barbarian Odoacer.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the administrative division and fall of the Western Roman Empire?
choices: Constantine moves the capital from Rome to Byzantium (Constantinople)
The Western Roman Empire ends in 476 CE
Diocletian divides the empire into two administrative realms

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Enduring Legacy of Roman Civilization
questions.lessonTitle: Roman Law and Its Enduring Influence
questions.lessonContent: Roman law began with the Twelve Tables in 450 BCE and developed over a thousand years, including decisions of judges, ideas of the Republic and Empire, and rulings of emperors. It encompassed public law (relationship of citizen to state), private civil law (relationships between people), and jus gentium (rights of foreigners). The Justinian Code (Corpus Juris Civilis) was compiled in the 6th century CE and encapsulated the previous thousand years of Roman legal development. This code still serves as the basis for civil law in many parts of Europe today.
questions.question: What was the Justinian Code and what is its modern significance?
questions.answer: The Justinian Code (Corpus Juris Civilis) was a compilation of Roman law by Emperor Justinian in the 6th century CE that encapsulated over 1000 years of legal development, and it still serves as the basis for civil law in many parts of Europe.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Enduring Legacy of Roman Civilization
questions.lessonTitle: Christianity's Transformation in the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Christianity started in the Roman province of Judea, and early Christians could travel freely throughout the empire due to the Pax Romana and Roman infrastructure. There was a significant number of Christians in Rome by 64 CE, when Nero blamed them for the fire that destroyed much of the city. The religion finally gained acceptance with the Edict of Milan in 313 CE, which legalized Christianity and granted religious toleration. After Constantine converted to Christianity and future emperors also became Christians, the religion transitioned from a persecuted sect to the state religion of the Roman Empire.
questions.question: Early Christians were able to travel freely throughout the Roman Empire primarily because of the Pax Romana and Roman infrastructure.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Enduring Legacy of Roman Civilization
questions.lessonContent: The Romans were renowned for their architectural achievements, which included public buildings such as amphitheaters, basilicas, government offices, palaces, public baths, and theaters. In terms of architectural style, the Romans copied basic styles from the Greeks, adapted the arch from the Etruscans, and pioneered the use of the dome and vault. A large part of Rome's success was due to the importance placed on building and maintaining infrastructure, including aqueducts, bridges, dams, harbors, and roads. The Colosseum, built by Emperor Vespasian, remains one of the most iconic examples of Roman amphitheater architecture.
questions.question: Which architectural element did the Romans adapt from the Etruscans?
questions.explanation: The Romans copied basic architectural styles from the Greeks, but they adapted the arch from the Etruscans, which they then used in construction projects such as aqueducts.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Enduring Legacy of Roman Civilization
questions.lessonContent: The rights of Roman citizenship underwent significant transformation during the Roman Empire. Initially, Roman citizenship was limited to Romans living in the city of Rome. Under Augustus, citizenship began to be extended to provincials living in the empire's territories. This process accelerated during the Pax Romana, when more and more provincials were granted official Roman citizenship. Finally, in 212 CE, Emperor Caracalla granted citizenship to all free men throughout the empire.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the expansion of Roman citizenship?
choices: Caracalla grants citizenship to all free men (212 CE)

results.file: How we built our multi-agent research system _ Anthropic.pdf

questions.lessonContent: A multi-agent system consists of multiple agents, defined as LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop, working together to accomplish complex tasks. Anthropic's Research system implements an orchestrator-worker pattern where a lead agent coordinates the entire research process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously. The subagents act as intelligent filters by iteratively using search tools to gather information before returning their findings to the lead agent for synthesis. This architecture enables parallel processing and allows each subagent to maintain its own context window for independent investigation.
questions.question: What architecture pattern does Anthropic's Research system use to coordinate multiple agents?

questions.lessonContent: Multi-agent systems consume significantly more tokens than single-agent chat interactions due to the parallel nature of subagent processing. According to Anthropic's internal data, agents typically use about 4 times more tokens than standard chat interactions. However, multi-agent systems, which involve coordinating multiple subagents with separate context windows, use approximately 15 times more tokens than chats. This high token usage is a trade-off for the increased capability and parallel processing that multi-agent systems provide.
questions.question: Multi-agent systems use about 4 times more tokens than chat interactions.

questions.lessonTitle: Primary Performance Driver in Multi-Agent Research
questions.lessonContent: Anthropic conducted analysis on the BrowseComp evaluation, which tests browsing agents' ability to locate hard-to-find information, to understand what drives performance in multi-agent systems. The analysis revealed that three factors explained 95% of the performance variance: token usage, number of tool calls, and model choice. Token usage by itself accounts for 80% of the variance, making it the dominant factor in performance. This finding validates multi-agent architectures that distribute work across agents with separate context windows, adding more capacity for parallel reasoning. The research showed that a multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on internal research evaluations.
questions.question: Which factor explains the largest portion of performance variance in multi-agent research systems according to Anthropic's analysis?
questions.explanation: Token usage by itself explains 80% of the performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation, making it the dominant factor compared to tool calls and model choice.

questions.lessonContent: When a lead agent decomposes queries for subagents, each subagent needs specific components to be effective: an objective, an output format, guidance on which tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries. Anthropic's early experiments showed that simple, short instructions like 'research the semiconductor shortage' were often too vague, causing subagents to misinterpret tasks or duplicate work. For example, one subagent explored the 2021 automotive chip crisis while two others investigated current 2025 supply chains without effective division of labor. Providing detailed task descriptions prevents agents from leaving gaps or failing to find necessary information.
questions.question: What four components must be included when describing a subtask to a subagent?
questions.answer: An objective, an output format, guidance on tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries

questions.lessonContent: In early agent development, changes tend to have dramatic impacts because there is abundant low-hanging fruit. A prompt tweak might boost success rates from 30% to 80%, making effect sizes large enough to spot with just a few test cases. Anthropic started with about 20 queries representing real usage patterns, and testing these queries often allowed them to clearly see the impact of changes. Many AI developer teams delay creating evaluations because they believe only large evals with hundreds of test cases are useful, but it is actually best to start with small-scale testing right away with a few examples rather than waiting.
questions.question: A team should wait to create evaluations until they can build a comprehensive eval with hundreds of test cases.

questions.lessonContent: Anthropic used an LLM judge to evaluate research outputs against criteria in a rubric: factual accuracy (whether claims match sources), citation accuracy (whether cited sources match the claims), completeness (whether all requested aspects are covered), source quality (whether it used primary sources over lower-quality secondary sources), and tool efficiency (whether it used the right tools a reasonable number of times). They experimented with multiple judges to evaluate each component, but found that a single LLM call with a prompt outputting scores from 0.0-1.0 and a pass-fail grade was most consistent and aligned with human judgments.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a criterion used in Anthropic's LLM-as-judge evaluation rubric?
questions.explanation: The five criteria are factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, and tool efficiency. Response creativity and originality is not mentioned as an evaluation criterion in the source content.

questions.lessonContent: When evaluating research agents, Anthropic starts with a small set of about 20 test queries to see the impact of changes quickly. They then use an LLM judge to evaluate each output against criteria, outputting scores from 0.0-1.0. Human evaluation is used to catch edge cases that automated evals miss, such as hallucinated answers on unusual queries or subtle source selection biases.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the prompt evaluation workflow for research agents?

questions.lessonContent: Agent systems are highly stateful webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously. This means that whenever Anthropic deploys updates, agents might be anywhere in their process. They need to prevent well-meaning code changes from breaking existing agents. They cannot update every agent to the new version at the same time. Instead, they use rainbow deployments to avoid disrupting running agents, by gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously.
questions.question: What deployment strategy does Anthropic use to avoid disrupting running agents when updating their multi-agent system?

questions.lessonContent: In traditional software, a bug might break a feature, degrade performance, or cause outages. In agentic systems, minor changes cascade into large behavioral changes, making it remarkably difficult to write code for complex agents that must maintain state in a long-running process. Agents can run for long periods of time, maintaining state across many tool calls. This means they need to durably execute code and handle errors along the way. They built systems that can resume from where the agent was when errors occurred, rather than restarting from the beginning which is expensive and frustrating for users.
questions.question: Agents maintain state across many tool calls and errors compound in agentic systems.

questions.lessonContent: Currently, Anthropic's lead agents execute subagents synchronously, waiting for each set of subagents to complete before proceeding. This simplifies coordination but creates bottlenecks in the information flow between agents. For instance, the lead agent cannot steer subagents, subagents cannot coordinate, and the entire system can be blocked while waiting for a single subagent to finish searching. Asynchronous execution would enable additional parallelism where agents work concurrently and create new subagents when needed. However, this asynchronicity adds challenges in result coordination, state consistency, and error propagation across the subagents.
questions.question: What issue does synchronous execution of subagents create in Anthropic's multi-agent research system?
choices: Faster response times for simple queries
Reduced token usage across the system
Bottlenecks in information flow between agents
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that synchronous execution 'creates bottlenecks in the information flow between agents' - the lead agent waits for each set of subagents to complete, which blocks the system.

questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage aims to improve the language model's base knowledge, specifically in the domain of coding. The research team evaluated several potential open-source base models including GLM-5, Kimi K2.5, and DeepSeek V3.2. These evaluations measured internal codebase perplexity, coding knowledge, and state tracking capabilities. The evaluations led the team to select Kimi K2.5 as the base model for Composer 2, which is a 1.04T parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 32B active parameters. This model was chosen due to its general strong performance as well as additional considerations such as its efficiency in the team's infrastructure.
questions.question: What was the total parameter count of the Kimi K2.5 model selected as the base model for Composer 2?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 extends Kimi K2.5 with a continued pretraining stage on a large code-dominated data mix to specialize the model on coding knowledge and capabilities. The team divides this stage into three distinct phases. They spend the bulk of compute at 32k token sequence length, which is the longest phase. This is followed by a shorter long-context extension phase that extends the sequence length to 256k tokens. Finally, there is a short supervised fine-tuning phase on targeted coding tasks. Training was performed in MXFP8 precision on NVIDIA B300s using the AdamW optimizer.
questions.question: During continued pretraining, the bulk of compute is spent at 32k token sequence length, followed by a 256k long-context extension phase.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 training uses a sophisticated parallelism approach combining multiple techniques. The model uses Context Parallelism (CP) as the primary long-context scaling axis, which requires less communication than Tensor Parallelism and improves compute efficiency by preserving full hidden dimensions. Additionally, Composer 2 introduces a more flexible expert-parallel design by decoupling Expert Parallelism (EP) from Tensor Parallelism. The team uses EP=8 and CP=2 for the continued pretraining phase, while using EP=8 and CP=8 for the reinforcement learning phase. This decoupling enables support for larger expert-parallel degrees and makes expert-grouped GEMMs more efficient with larger per-rank token batches.
questions.question: What parallelism configuration (Expert Parallelism and Context Parallelism degrees) is used during the continued pretraining phase?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that the team uses EP=8 and CP=2 for the continued pretraining phase, distinguishing it from the RL phase which uses EP=8 and CP=8.

questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage for Composer 2 is divided into three distinct phases. First, the bulk of compute is spent at 32k token sequence length to build foundational coding knowledge. Following this, a shorter long-context extension phase extends the model's context window to 256k sequence length. Finally, a short SFT phase trains the model on targeted coding tasks to prepare it for downstream reinforcement learning.
questions.question: What is the correct order of phases in the Composer 2 continued pretraining process?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Reinforcement Learning and Agent Behavior
questions.lessonContent: To incentivize the model to produce solutions quickly on easy requests while allowing it to think longer on hard requests, a concave down and increasing nonlinear length penalty is applied to the reward. The formula is: Clength{k,q}(x) = ((1 + kx)^(1-q) - 1) / (k(1 - q)), where k and q are hyperparameters which define the curvature of the penalty. The input x is a weighted combination of thinking tokens, tool calling tokens, tool output tokens, final message tokens, number of tool calls, and number of turns of a rollout. This nonlinearity reflects that on easy tasks achievable with only a few tool calls, every additional bit of effort is felt more acutely than in long-horizon tasks where the agent might iterate for hundreds of tool calls.
questions.question: What are the two hyperparameters in the nonlinear length penalty formula used to incentivize efficient agent behavior?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Reinforcement Learning and Agent Behavior
questions.lessonContent: Our reinforcement learning pipeline is built around learning from large-scale policy gradients while maintaining stability. They use a policy gradient algorithm with multiple samples per prompt and a fixed group size. They operate in the single-epoch regime, meaning the same prompt is never trained on twice. They utilize Adam as the underlying optimizer and update the full parameter set. RL training operates in a highly asynchronous regime with independent training and rollout generation workers. A key strategy to maintain stability is minimizing how off-policy the samples become through fast weight synchronization and in-flight weight updates, where inference workers can update weights mid-rollout.
questions.question: In Composer 2's asynchronous RL training, the same prompt is never trained on twice.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Reinforcement Learning and Agent Behavior
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is trained by reinforcement learning on a large set of coding tasks run in environments that emulate real Cursor sessions. They create a problem distribution that reflects the most common use cases.
