According to Figure 3 in the report, the task categories include Iterate On Feature, Debugging, New Feature, Refactor, Understanding Codebase, Documentation, Testing, Code Review, Optimize, Devops, Migration, Deletion, and Other. This training distribution captures many aspects of software engineering that are absent from popular AI coding benchmarks. In later stages of training, simple heuristics such as number of turns and thinking tokens of rollouts are used to upsample increasingly harder data points.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed as a task category in the RL training distribution for Composer 2?
questions.explanation: Code Compilation is not listed as a task category. The actual categories include Debugging, Refactor, and Devops, along with Iterate On Feature, New Feature, Understanding Codebase, Documentation, Testing, Code Review, Optimize, Migration, Deletion, and Other.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Reinforcement Learning and Agent Behavior
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 trains using reinforcement learning on coding tasks by iterating through a systematic process. First, the system selects a problem from the task distribution, which reflects common software engineering use cases like debugging, new features, refactoring, and testing. Next, multiple rollouts are generated from the agent policy, with each rollout containing a series of actions such as file edits, shell commands, and searches. Finally, the solutions are evaluated based on criteria like correctness, code quality, and adherence to software engineering principles, with rewards computed to guide policy improvements.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Composer 2 reinforcement learning training loop?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 employs different parallelism configurations for its continued pretraining and reinforcement learning phases. During continued pretraining, the system uses Expert Parallelism (EP) of 8 and Context Parallelism (CP) of 2. However, for the RL phase, the configuration changes to EP=8 and CP=8. This change in Context Parallelism from 2 to 8 is significant because CP requires less communication than Tensor Parallelism and improves compute efficiency by preserving full hidden dimensions in various projections.
questions.question: What Expert Parallelism and Context Parallelism degrees are used during the RL phase in Composer 2?

questions.lessonContent: CursorBench is an internal evaluation suite designed to reflect the true distribution of software engineering tasks. Compared to public benchmarks like SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual, CursorBench tasks require substantially more extensive code modifications with a median of 181 lines changed versus just 7-10 lines for public benchmarks. Additionally, CursorBench prompts are more under-specified with a median description length of only 390 characters compared to 1,185-3,055 characters for public benchmarks. This combination of broad execution scope and high intent ambiguity accurately reflects real-world software engineering difficulty.
questions.question: True or False: CursorBench tasks require fewer lines of code changes on average compared to SWE-bench Verified tasks.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 achieves strong performance across multiple evaluation benchmarks. On CursorBench-3, the model achieves 61.3% accuracy. On SWE-bench Multilingual, Composer 2 scores 73.7%, and on Terminal-Bench it achieves 61.7%. These results represent significant improvements over previous Composer versions, with Composer 1.5 achieving 44.2% on CursorBench, 65.9% on SWE-bench Multilingual, and 47.9% on Terminal-Bench. The base model Kimi K2.5 only achieved 36.0% on CursorBench, 65.1% on SWE-bench Multilingual, and 47.3% on Terminal-Bench.
questions.question: Which of the following benchmark scores is achieved by Composer 2?
questions.explanation: Composer 2 achieves 61.3% on CursorBench-3 according to Table 1 in the technical report, representing a 37% relative improvement over Composer 1.5.

questions.lessonContent: The Composer 2 RL training infrastructure uses a decoupled service architecture. When a training prompt requires a coding environment, the trainer first sends a request to a global service. This service then routes the request to an underlying Anyrun cluster, which is responsible for managing pods that run Firecracker VMs capable of hosting full development environments. Within the cluster, Anyrun managers schedule pods, scale cloud compute across multiple regions, and perform state reconciliation to manage hundreds of thousands of pods per cluster.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the environment creation workflow for Composer 2 RL training?

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Your Environment
questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. This makes it an ideal place for documenting common bash commands, core files and utility functions, code style guidelines, testing instructions, repository etiquette, developer environment setup, and any unexpected behaviors or warnings particular to your project. You can place CLAUDE.md files in several locations: the root of your repo (or wherever you run claude from), any parent of the directory where you run claude, any child of the directory, or your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md which applies to all your Claude sessions. When you run the /init command, Claude will automatically generate a CLAUDE.md file for you. The file has no required format, but it is recommended to keep it concise and human-readable.
questions.question: What is the name of the special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation?

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Your Environment
questions.lessonTitle: Configuring Allowed Tools in Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code is designed with a deliberately conservative approach to prioritize safety. By default, Claude Code requests permission for any action that might modify your system, including file writes, many bash commands, and MCP tools. You can customize the allowlist to permit additional tools that you know are safe, or to allow potentially unsafe tools that are easy to undo. There are four ways to manage allowed tools: selecting "Always allow" when prompted during a session, using the /permissions command after starting Claude Code, manually editing your .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json, or using the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions.
questions.question: By default, Claude Code requests permission for actions that might modify your system, such as file writes and bash commands.

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Your Environment
questions.lessonTitle: MCP Server Configuration in Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code can connect to any number of MCP servers to access their tools in three ways: in project config (available when running Claude Code in that directory), in global config (available in all projects), or in a checked-in .mcp.json file available to anyone working in your codebase. For example, you can add Puppeteer and Sentry servers to your .mcp.json file so that every engineer working on your repo can use these tools out of the box. The MCP configuration allows you to extend Claude's capabilities by connecting to external servers that provide additional functionality.
questions.question: How can MCP servers be configured in Claude Code?
choices: Only in the root directory of the project
Only in the Claude Code installation folder
In project config, global config, or a checked-in .mcp.json file
questions.explanation: According to the source content, MCP servers can be configured in three ways: in project config (available when running Claude Code in that directory), in global config (available in all projects), or in a checked-in .mcp.json file that makes tools available to anyone working in the codebase.

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Your Environment
questions.lessonContent: When customizing your Claude Code environment, the first steps involve creating and configuring a CLAUDE.md file. You begin by creating the CLAUDE.md file itself, which serves as a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. Next, you choose where to place this file, deciding on the root of your repo, a parent directory, or your home folder. Finally, you add content to the CLAUDE.md file, documenting common bash commands, code style guidelines, and testing instructions that you want Claude to remember.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps for setting up a CLAUDE.md file in your Claude Code environment?

questions.lessonContent: The 'Explore, plan, code, commit' workflow is a versatile pattern that suits many problems. In the first step, you ask Claude to read relevant files, images, or URLs, providing either general pointers or specific filenames, but explicitly telling it not to write any code yet. This is also the part of the workflow where you should consider strong use of subagents for complex problems, especially early in a conversation or task. Telling Claude to use subagents to verify details or investigate particular questions tends to preserve context availability without much downside in terms of lost efficiency. The second step involves asking Claude to make a plan for how to approach the specific problem, and if the results seem reasonable, you can have Claude create a document or a GitHub issue with its plan so you can reset to this spot if the implementation isn't what you want.
questions.question: What is the name of the workflow that involves exploring, planning, coding, and committing?

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code offers a Safe YOLO mode that allows you to bypass all permission checks using the --dangerously-skip-permissions flag. This enables Claude to work uninterrupted until completion. The feature works well for workflows like fixing lint errors or generating boilerplate code. However, letting Claude run arbitrary commands is risky and can result in data loss, system corruption, or even data exfiltration through prompt injection attacks. To minimize these risks, the documentation recommends using --dangerously-skip-permissions in a container without internet access, following a reference implementation using Docker Dev Containers.
questions.question: True or false: The --dangerously-skip-permissions flag allows Claude to work without permission checks and is recommended for use in containers without internet access.

questions.lessonContent: For running multiple Claude instances in parallel, there are two primary approaches. The first is having multiple checkouts of your repo in separate folders, opening each folder in separate terminal tabs, and starting Claude in each folder with different tasks while cycling through to check progress and approve or deny permission requests. The second approach uses git worktrees, which allow you to check out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories, with each worktree having its own working directory with isolated files while sharing the same Git history and reflog. Git worktrees offer a lighter-weight alternative to multiple checkouts, enabling you to run multiple Claude sessions simultaneously on different parts of your project.
questions.question: Which approach provides a lighter-weight alternative for running multiple Claude sessions simultaneously on different parts of your project?
choices: Using separate Claude instances in different terminal tabs without any git setup
Using a single Claude session with /clear command to switch between tasks
Using multiple git checkouts in separate folders
Using git worktrees to check out multiple branches into separate directories
questions.explanation: Git worktrees allow you to check out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories, with each worktree having its own working directory with isolated files while sharing the same Git history and reflog, making it a lighter-weight alternative to multiple checkouts.

questions.lessonContent: In the test-driven development workflow, Claude Code follows a specific sequence. First, you ask Claude to write tests based on expected input/output pairs, being explicit about doing test-driven development so it avoids creating mock implementations. Then, you tell Claude to run the tests and confirm they fail - explicitly telling it not to write any implementation code at this stage. Finally, you ask Claude to write code that passes the tests, instructing it not to modify the tests and telling it to keep going until all tests pass.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the test-driven development workflow?
choices: Run tests to confirm they fail
Write code to make tests pass

questions.lessonTitle: Headless Mode Purpose and Use Cases
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code includes headless mode for non-interactive contexts like CI, pre-commit hooks, build scripts, and automation. Use the -p flag with a prompt to enable headless mode, and --output-format stream-json for streaming JSON output. Note that headless mode does not persist between sessions; you have to trigger it each session. This mode is particularly useful for powering automations triggered by GitHub events, such as when a new issue is created in your repository.
questions.question: What flag is used to enable headless mode in Claude Code?

questions.lessonContent: A simple but effective multi-agent approach is to have one Claude write code while another reviews or tests it. Similar to working with multiple engineers, sometimes having separate context is beneficial. The workflow involves: first use Claude to write code, then run /clear or start a second Claude in another terminal, have the second Claude review the first Claude's work, start another Claude or /clear again to read both the code and review feedback, and finally have this Claude edit the code based on the feedback. This separation often yields better results than having a single Claude handle everything.
questions.question: True or false: Using multiple Claude instances for writing and reviewing code typically yields better results than a single Claude handling everything.

questions.lessonContent: Headless mode with a custom harness integrates Claude Code programmatically into larger workflows while leveraging its built-in tools and system prompt. There are two primary patterns for using headless mode: fanning out handles large migrations or analyses by having Claude write a script to generate a task list, then looping through tasks calling Claude programmatically for each with specific tools. Pipelining integrates Claude into existing data or processing pipelines by calling claude -p with a prompt and piping the output to the next step of your processing pipeline. JSON output can help provide structure for easier automated processing.
questions.question: Which pattern involves calling Claude programmatically in a loop to handle large numbers of similar tasks like file migrations?
questions.explanation: Fanning out handles large migrations or analyses by having Claude generate a task list and then looping through tasks, calling Claude programmatically for each task with specific tools and allowed actions.

questions.lessonTitle: Git Worktrees for Parallel Claude Sessions
questions.lessonContent: Git worktrees provide a lighter-weight alternative for running multiple Claude sessions simultaneously on different parts of your project. Each worktree has its own working directory with isolated files, while sharing the same Git history and reflog. To set this up, you first create a worktree using git worktree add with a branch name. Then you launch Claude in each worktree by navigating to the worktree directory and running claude. Finally, you create additional worktrees as needed by repeating these steps in new terminal tabs, allowing each Claude instance to work on independent tasks without waiting for other's changes or dealing with merge conflicts.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps for using git worktrees to run multiple Claude sessions in parallel?

questions.lessonTitle: Together Embeddings: Available Models and Cost Efficiency
questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint was released on January 11, 2024, offering 8 leading embedding models. These include models from the MTEB leaderboard such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models, as well as the newly released M2-BERT retrieval models for long context with options of 2k, 8k, and 32k context lengths. The platform claims these models are up to 4x cheaper than other popular platforms. The endpoint provides state-of-the-art performance in MTEB benchmarks, with some models outperforming both OpenAI's ada-002 and Cohere's Embed-v3.
questions.question: How many embedding models are available in the Together Embeddings endpoint?

questions.lessonTitle: Long Context Capabilities of M2-BERT Retrieval Models
questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint includes M2-BERT retrieval models that are specifically designed for long context tasks. These models support context lengths of 2k, 8k, and 32k tokens. According to the documentation, these M2-BERT retrieval models significantly outperform other closed models in long context retrieval tasks. This capability allows users to generate embeddings for long documents without splitting them into many short chunks while containing more meaningful contexts in the embeddings.
questions.question: M2-BERT retrieval models support context lengths of 2k, 8k, and 32k tokens.

questions.lessonContent: Text embeddings provide a measure of the similarity or relatedness of given text queries. This mathematical representation of text enables various downstream applications in AI and data science. Embeddings are commonly used for clustering similar documents together based on their semantic content. They also power semantic search systems that can find relevant documents even when exact keyword matches are absent. Additionally, embeddings enable classification tasks by providing numerical representations that can be used with machine learning classifiers.
questions.question: Which of the following is a use case for text embeddings?
questions.explanation: Semantic search is explicitly listed as one of the primary use cases for text embeddings in the source content. The document states that embeddings are used for clustering, semantic search, and classification.

questions.lessonContent: In the data visualization example from the Together Embeddings endpoint, the workflow involves several key steps. First, you generate embeddings using the Together API with a model like M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K. Next, you extract embeddings from the API response for each data sample. Finally, you transform the high-dimensional embeddings (768 dimensions for M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K) using tSNE to reduce them to 2D for plotting. This sequential process allows you to visualize text data from different sources in a two-dimensional space.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Together Embeddings data visualization workflow?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint provides full OpenAI compatibility, allowing developers who have built applications following the OpenAI API to easily migrate their code. To use this compatibility feature, you configure the OpenAI client with a specific base_url pointing to Together's API endpoint. The base_url is set to "https://api.together.xyz/api/v1/embeddings" and requires your Together API key for authentication. This setup enables you to use the same OpenAI client patterns you already know while accessing Together's embedding models.
questions.question: What is the base_url configuration required to make the Together Embeddings endpoint compatible with the OpenAI client library?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint supports full OpenAI compatibility, which means you can use the standard OpenAI client library to interact with Together's embedding models. This compatibility makes it easier for developers who are already familiar with the OpenAI API to switch to Together's platform without rewriting their application code. The integration uses the familiar client.embeddings.create() method to generate embeddings. This approach simplifies migration from other platforms that use the OpenAI standard.
questions.question: The Together Embeddings endpoint has full OpenAI compatibility, allowing developers to use the standard OpenAI client library with their existing code.

questions.lessonTitle: Compatible Client Method for Embedding Creation
questions.lessonContent: When using the OpenAI compatibility feature of the Together Embeddings endpoint, developers use the standard OpenAI client library to create embeddings. The client is initialized with the Together API key and the specific base_url for Together's API. To generate embeddings, you call the client.embeddings.create() method, passing the input text and the model name as parameters. This method returns embedding data that includes the actual embedding vector for the provided text. The model parameter specifies which embedding model to use, such as "togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-32k-retrieval".
questions.question: Which method is used to create embeddings when using the OpenAI-compatible interface with Together Embeddings?
questions.explanation: The correct method is client.embeddings.create(), which follows the standard OpenAI API pattern and returns embedding data including the embedding vector for the input text.

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Systems and Practical Applications
questions.lessonTitle: Frameworks for Building RAG with Together Embeddings
questions.lessonContent: One of the most popular use cases of embeddings models is building a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system. You can build RAG using the Together API and popular vector databases such as MongoDB, Pinecone, and Chroma, or by leveraging frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex. The blog provides deep-dive tutorials on how to build RAG using Together with MongoDB, using Together with LangChain, or using Together with LlamaIndex. These frameworks integrate with the Together Embeddings endpoint to enable efficient retrieval and generation workflows.
questions.question: Which two frameworks are mentioned for building RAG systems with Together Embeddings?

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Systems and Practical Applications
questions.lessonContent: Retrieval Augmented Generation, or RAG, aims to overcome limitations of generative AI models, such as a lack of knowledge from unseen data, by finding relevant information from a given knowledge base through embeddings and providing the information to a generative model. This approach allows AI systems to access and utilize information beyond their original training data, making them more accurate and contextually aware. RAG systems combine the power of embeddings for semantic search with large language models for text generation.
questions.question: RAG systems overcome generative AI limitations by finding relevant information from a knowledge base through embeddings and providing it to a generative model.

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Systems and Practical Applications
questions.lessonContent: The dimension of embedding vectors is usually too large to easily visualize in two-dimensional space. For the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model, the embedding dimension is 768. To plot each data example in 2D, the code uses t-SNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding) to transform the high-dimensional embedding vectors into a lower-dimensional representation that can be easily plotted and interpreted. The visualization example in the documentation shows how to process sample data from various domains of RedPajama-v1.
questions.question: What is the embedding dimension of the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that for M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K, the embedding dimension is 768.

results.file: How does image compression work_ _ Lee Robinson.pdf

questions.lessonTitle: Understanding Pixel Composition in Digital Images
questions.lessonContent: Images appear smooth and continuous, but when magnified they reveal a grid of tiny colored squares called pixels. Each pixel contains three numerical values representing the intensity of red, green, and blue light needed to create its color. These color values range from 0, indicating no presence of that color, to 255, representing maximum intensity. For example, a pixel with RGB values (255, 147, 41) would display an orange color. A standard HD screenshot with dimensions of 1920 × 1080 pixels contains over 2 million individual pixels.
questions.question: How many numerical values does each pixel contain, and what do these values represent?
questions.answer: Three values representing red, green, and blue (RGB)

questions.lessonTitle: The Fundamental Trade-off in Image Compression
questions.lessonContent: There are two fundamental approaches to making image files smaller. Lossy compression, used by formats like JPEG, works by throwing away data that humans are unlikely to notice, such as subtle color variations. Lossless compression, used by formats like PNG, preserves every single pixel perfectly while still reducing file size through clever encoding techniques. These two approaches power JPEG, PNG, ZIP files, web traffic, and most of the internet. When using lossy compression, the original pixel data cannot be recovered because it has been permanently discarded during the compression process.
questions.question: With lossy compression, the original pixel data cannot be recovered after compression.

questions.lessonContent: To understand why compression is necessary, consider the raw data size of an uncompressed image. An HD screenshot with dimensions of 1920 × 1080 pixels contains exactly 2,073,600 pixels. Since each pixel requires 3 bytes of storage (one byte each for red, green, and blue values), the total uncompressed size calculates to 2,073,600 multiplied by 3 bytes, which equals 6,220,800 bytes or approximately 6.2 megabytes. This substantial file size demonstrates why compression algorithms are essential for efficient storage and transmission of images across the internet.
questions.question: What is the approximate uncompressed file size of an HD screenshot (1920 × 1080 pixels) in megabytes?
questions.explanation: 1920 × 1080 = 2,073,600 pixels. Each pixel needs 3 bytes (RGB), so 2,073,600 × 3 = 6,220,800 bytes ≈ 6.2 MB.

questions.lessonContent: The PNG compression pipeline uses three sequential techniques to shrink image files without losing quality. First, Filtering predicts each pixel from its neighbors and stores the differences rather than the raw values. After filtering, LZ77 Pattern Find scans the data for repeated sequences and replaces them with compact back-references. Finally, Huffman Encode assigns shorter binary codes to values that appear more frequently, reducing the overall bit count. These three steps must be applied in this exact order to achieve optimal compression.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the PNG lossless image compression pipeline?

questions.lessonContent: JPEG takes a clever approach to compressing photographs. After converting from RGB to a format that separates brightness from color, JPEG divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks. Each block is then transformed into frequency components, where low frequencies represent smooth gradients and high frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges. Since photographs are mostly smooth gradients, most of the visual information ends up in just a few low-frequency components. JPEG then throws away the high-frequency details that human eyes won't typically notice, keeping the smooth parts intact.
questions.question: What block size does JPEG use when transforming image data?

questions.lessonContent: Lossy compression exploits specific characteristics of human vision. Our eyes resolve brightness in fine detail very accurately, but they tend to blur color information together. We notice sharp edges clearly, but we won't notice if colors are slightly off from the original. JPEG takes advantage of this by reducing color resolution since human eyes are less sensitive to color variations than to brightness variations. This selective reduction allows JPEG to achieve significant file size reduction while maintaining perceived image quality.
questions.question: JPEG reduces color resolution because human eyes are more sensitive to brightness than color.

questions.lessonTitle: Trade-off Between File Size and Quality
questions.lessonContent: When using lossy compression like JPEG, there is a significant trade-off between file size and image quality. At high quality settings, the difference between the original and compressed image is barely noticeable to the human eye. However, when compression is cranked up, visible artifacts appear where fine details are lost, often appearing as blocking artifacts. Despite this loss of detail, the trade-off is often worth it because lossy compression can achieve 10-20x smaller files with minimal visible difference compared to the original.
questions.question: What compression ratio can lossy compression achieve while maintaining minimal visible difference?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that lossy compression produces files that are 10-20x smaller with minimal visible difference.

questions.lessonContent: In lossy JPEG compression, the process begins by converting the RGB image to YCbCr format, which separates brightness from color information. This separation allows the algorithm to reduce color resolution since human vision is more sensitive to brightness details than color variations. The image is then divided into 8x8 pixel blocks for processing.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the initial JPEG color processing pipeline?

questions.lessonContent: In lossless PNG compression, instead of storing each pixel value directly, we store how much each pixel differs from its neighbor. Adjacent pixels in images like a blue sky are usually very similar (128, 130, 132, 134...). Rather than storing these full values, the algorithm predicts each pixel based on its neighbor and stores only the small difference. These difference values are typically small numbers, which are much easier to compress than the original pixel values.
questions.question: In lossless compression, what does the prediction step store instead of the actual pixel values?

questions.lessonContent: PNG files use a structured chunk-based format where each chunk contains a specific type of data. One important safety feature is that each chunk includes a CRC-32 checksum, which is a mathematical fingerprint of the chunk's data. When you open a PNG file, your computer recalculates this fingerprint and compares it to the stored value. If the checksums don't match, the file is damaged and cannot be properly decoded.
questions.question: The CRC-32 checksum in PNG chunks allows the computer to detect when a file is damaged.

questions.lessonContent: After prediction, the LZ77 algorithm scans for repeated patterns in the data. It maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data, allowing it to reference any pattern within that window instead of storing repeated values. For example, instead of storing the sequence 0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 2 repeatedly, it can say 'go back 5 values and copy 5,' replacing the repeated sequence with a tiny reference that takes much less space.
questions.question: What is the size of the sliding window that LZ77 uses when finding repeated patterns in lossless compression?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states: 'LZ77 maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data.'

questions.lessonContent: The lossless compression pipeline uses three main techniques to shrink image files while preserving every pixel. First, filtering or prediction compares each pixel to its neighbors and stores only the differences, since adjacent pixels are usually similar. Second, LZ77 pattern finding scans the data for repeated sequences and replaces them with compact back-references. Third, Huffman encoding assigns shorter binary codes to frequently occurring values and longer codes to rare ones, similar to how Morse code gives common letters shorter signals.
questions.question: What is the correct order of the three core compression techniques used in PNG lossless compression?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Octavian was sole ruler of Rome after his forces defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium. The Senate gave him the name "Augustus," meaning "most high." In 23 BCE, Octavian, now referred to as Augustus, was made consul for life by the Senate. He was also made "Princeps," meaning "first citizen" - which is the origin of the word "prince" - and "Imperator," meaning "successful general" - which is the origin of the word "emperor."
questions.question: What name did the Senate give to Octavian after his victory at the Battle of Actium?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Rome controlled the entire Mediterranean region and beyond, establishing what became known as the Pax Romana or Roman Peace. This complete control meant almost no warfare throughout the region. This peace lasted nearly 200 years, from the reign of Augustus beginning around 27 BCE until the death of Marcus Aurelius in 180 CE. During this time, more and more provincials were granted official Roman citizenship.
questions.question: The Pax Romana, the period of Roman Peace, lasted approximately 200 years.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Augustus attempted to reform public morals by promoting family life, though this was largely unsuccessful. He began the practice of declaring emperors gods and of picking their own successors. He built and maintained the empire's infrastructure, including roads, and encouraged the growth of business. Augustus established fire and police departments for Rome and established a strong money system. He extended citizenship to more and more provincials. He famously said he "found Rome a city of bricks and left it a city of marble."
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT an achievement or action of Augustus during his reign?
choices: Transforming Rome from bricks to marble
questions.explanation: The Colosseum was built by Emperor Vespasian, not Augustus. Augustus did transform Rome from a city of bricks to a city of marble, established fire and police departments, and extended citizenship to provincials.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: After Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium, he became the sole ruler of Rome. The Senate then gave him the name 'Augustus,' meaning 'most high.' Finally, in 23 BCE, Octavian (now Augustus) was made consul for life by the Senate.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in Octavian's rise to power as Augustus?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Transformation of the Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Principle of Primus Inter Pares
questions.lessonContent: Augustus and later emperors tried to maintain the façade that they were elected officials rather than dictators. Being "first among equals" gave the illusion that an emperor was the most prestigious and important member of the Roman Senate, but that each senator was simultaneously equally important. This Latin phrase is "primus inter pares." In reality, the Roman emperors ruled with little input from anyone else, despite the pretense of equality among senators.
questions.question: What does the Latin phrase "primus inter pares" mean?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Transformation of the Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Year of the Four Emperors
questions.lessonContent: Following the death of Emperor Nero in 68 CE, Rome experienced a brief period of civil war known as the Year of the Four Emperors. In 69 CE, four emperors ruled in quick succession: Galba, Otho, Vitellius, and finally Vespasian. This rapid succession of rulers illustrated the fundamental problems of imperial succession in the Roman Empire, as there was no clear, orderly method for determining who would become the next emperor.
questions.question: The Year of the Four Emperors (69 CE) involved four emperors ruling in succession, illustrating the problems of imperial succession.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: The Transformation of the Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Second Jewish Revolt Under Hadrian
questions.lessonContent: Under Emperor Hadrian (117-138 CE), the Romans put down the Second Jewish Revolt, also known as the Bar Kokhba Revolt, which occurred from 132-136 CE. This revolt was led by Simon Bar Kokhba, a man many Jewish people believed to be the messiah. After the revolt was defeated, Jews were forced to leave Jerusalem, and many historians date this as the official start of the Jewish Diaspora, when Jews scattered throughout the Mediterranean world and beyond.
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the Second Jewish Revolt under Emperor Hadrian?
choices: It was led by Emperor Titus and resulted in the construction of the Colosseum.
It was a peaceful protest that successfully established an independent Jewish kingdom.
It was the first Jewish revolt against Roman rule and resulted in the destruction of the First Temple.
It was led by Simon Bar Kokhba and resulted in the forced migration of Jews from Jerusalem, beginning the Jewish Diaspora.
questions.explanation: The Second Jewish Revolt (Bar Kokhba Revolt) occurred from 132-136 CE, was led by Simon Bar Kokhba (whom many believed to be the messiah), and after defeat, Jews were forced to leave Jerusalem, marking the official start of the Jewish Diaspora.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall and Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonContent: Justinian was a powerful emperor of the Eastern (Byzantine) empire headquartered at Constantinople. He married Theodora, an intelligent courtesan, and managed to reunite the Eastern and Western empires for a brief period. Justinian's most significant accomplishment was rewriting Roman law into what became known as the Corpus Juris Civilis, or the Justinian Code. This compilation of Roman law still forms the basis for civil law in several countries today.
questions.question: What was the name of Justinian's rewritten Roman law that serves as the basis for civil law in many countries today?
questions.answer: Corpus Juris Civilis (or the Justinian Code)

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall and Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonTitle: The Division of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Diocletian believed that dividing the empire for administrative purposes would strengthen it. In 285 CE, he divided the empire into two administrative realms: the Roman (Western) Empire and the Byzantine (Eastern) Empire. However, Diocletian was wrong in his prediction. Once Constantine set up Constantinople as a capital city in 312 CE, the east/west split deepened considerably, leading to the eventual creation of two separate empires.
questions.question: Diocletian divided the empire into two administrative realms in 285 CE to strengthen the empire.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall and Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonTitle: The End of the Roman Empires
questions.lessonContent: The Western Roman Empire ended officially in 476 CE when the last emperor, Romulus Augustus, was deposed by a barbarian named Odoacer. The Eastern (Byzantine) Empire, however, lasted much longer, surviving until 1453 when it was conquered by the Ottoman Turks. These two different end dates demonstrate how the division of the empire created two very different fates for the Eastern and Western halves of Roman civilization.
questions.question: When did the Western (Roman) Empire officially end?
choices: 476 CE when Romulus Augustus was deposed by Odoacer
312 CE when Constantine moved the capital to Constantinople
1453 CE when the Ottoman Turks conquered Constantinople
285 CE when Diocletian divided the empire
questions.explanation: The Western Roman Empire officially ended in 476 CE when the last emperor, Romulus Augustus, was deposed by the barbarian Odoacer. The Eastern (Byzantine) Empire lasted until 1453 CE.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall and Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonTitle: The Rise of Christianity in the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Christianity began in the Roman province of Judea during Augustus's reign, when Jesus was born. In 64 CE, Emperor Nero blamed Christians for the Great Fire of Rome, leading to persecution. Later, according to tradition, Paul of Tarsus used his Roman citizenship to have his criminal trial relocated to Rome from Caesarea in the 60s CE. These three events represent key moments in the early spread and challenges of Christianity within the Roman Empire.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the rise of Christianity in the Roman Empire?

results.file: How we built our multi-agent research system _ Anthropic.pdf

questions.lessonContent: A multi-agent system consists of multiple agents, which are LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop, working together to accomplish complex tasks. In the Research system, an agent plans a research process based on user queries and then uses tools to create parallel agents that search for information simultaneously. Each subagent operates with its own context window, exploring different aspects of a question before condensing the most important tokens for the lead research agent. This architecture enables separation of concerns through distinct tools, prompts, and exploration trajectories, which reduces path dependency and enables thorough investigations.
questions.question: According to the source content, what is a multi-agent system?
questions.answer: A multi-agent system consists of multiple agents (LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop) working together

questions.lessonContent: Multi-agent research systems excel particularly for breadth-first queries that involve pursuing multiple independent directions simultaneously. In the Anthropic system, the lead agent spawns subagents to explore different aspects of a query in parallel. Each subagent independently performs web searches, evaluates tool results using interleaved thinking, and returns findings to the lead agent. The lead agent then synthesizes these results and decides whether more research is needed. This parallel approach allows the system to cover more information than sequential searches and complete complex research tasks in minutes instead of hours.
questions.question: Multi-agent research systems are designed primarily for breadth-first queries that involve pursuing multiple independent directions simultaneously.

questions.lessonContent: The Research system uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the entire research process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously. The lead agent acts as an orchestrator that decomposes queries into subtasks and describes them to subagents, with each subagent needing an objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries. The system also includes a CitationAgent at the end that processes documents and research reports to identify specific locations for citations.
questions.question: What architecture pattern does the Anthropic Research system use?
choices: Mesh pattern where all agents communicate directly with each other
Orchestrator-worker pattern where a lead agent coordinates while delegating to specialized subagents
Hub-and-spoke pattern where a central agent distributes tasks evenly
Pipeline pattern where agents process data in sequential stages
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states: 'Our Research system uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel.'

questions.lessonContent: In Anthropic's multi-agent system, the lead agent decomposes user queries into subtasks and describes them to subagents. Each subagent requires four specific components: an objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries. Without detailed task descriptions, agents tend to duplicate work, leave gaps in research, or fail to find necessary information. Anthropic found that simple, short instructions like 'research the semiconductor shortage' were often vague enough that subagents misinterpreted the task or performed identical searches as other agents.
questions.question: According to the content, what are the four components required for each subagent task description?
questions.answer: An objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries

questions.lessonContent: Anthropic's experience building multi-agent systems revealed that the best prompts are not strict instructions but rather frameworks for collaboration. These frameworks define the division of labor, problem-solving approaches, and effort budgets for the agents. This approach focuses on instilling good heuristics rather than rigid rules, allowing agents to adapt flexibly to different research scenarios.
questions.question: True or false: Anthropic found that the best prompts for multi-agent systems contain strict instructions that agents must follow exactly.

questions.lessonContent: Anthropic embedded scaling rules directly into their prompts to help the lead agent allocate resources efficiently based on query complexity. According to their documented approach: simple fact-finding requires just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls, direct comparisons might need 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each, and complex research might use more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities. These explicit guidelines were developed to prevent overinvestment in simple queries, which was a common failure mode in early versions of their system.
questions.question: According to Anthropic's scaling rules embedded in prompts, how many subagents and tool calls are recommended for direct comparison tasks?
choices: 1 agent with more than 20 tool calls
More than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities
questions.explanation: According to the source content, direct comparisons might need 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each, as part of the scaling rules Anthropic embedded in their prompts to allocate resources efficiently based on query complexity.

questions.lessonContent: When engineering prompts for multi-agent research systems, Anthropic follows a sequential approach to prompt development. First, they build agent simulations using their Console with exact prompts and tools to understand agent effects and identify failure modes. Next, they teach the orchestrator how to delegate by providing detailed task descriptions including objectives, output formats, and clear boundaries. Finally, they define scaling rules that specify appropriate effort levels for different query complexities, from simple fact-finding to complex research requiring multiple subagents.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in Anthropic's prompt engineering process for multi-agent systems?
choices: Build agent simulations to understand agent effects
Teach the orchestrator how to delegate

questions.lessonTitle: Stateful Error Handling in Agentic Systems
questions.lessonContent: In agentic systems, minor changes cascade into large behavioral changes, which makes it remarkably difficult to write code for complex agents that must maintain state in a long-running process. Agents are stateful and errors compound because they can run for long periods of time, maintaining state across many tool calls. This means that minor system failures can be catastrophic for agents without effective mitigations. When errors occur, restarts are expensive and frustrating for users, so Anthropic built systems that can resume from where the agent was when errors occurred. They also let the agent know when a tool is failing and let it adapt, which works surprisingly well. The approach combines the adaptability of AI agents built on Claude with deterministic safeguards like retry logic and regular checkpoints.
questions.question: According to the content, what two components does Anthropic combine to handle errors gracefully in agentic systems?
questions.answer: Deterministic safeguards (retry logic and regular checkpoints) combined with the adaptability of AI agents built on Claude

questions.lessonTitle: Deployment Methods for Stateful Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: Agent systems are highly stateful webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously in production. This creates a deployment challenge: whenever updates are deployed, agents might be anywhere in their process, so well-meaning code changes could break existing agents. Anthropic cannot update every agent to the new version at the same time. Instead, they use rainbow deployments to avoid disrupting running agents by gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously. This ensures that agents in the middle of research tasks are not interrupted when system updates occur.
questions.question: True or false: Anthropic uses rainbow deployments to update their agent system without disrupting agents currently in the middle of tasks.

questions.lessonTitle: Token Usage Differences Across System Types
questions.lessonContent: Anthropic analyzed their internal data and found significant differences in token consumption across different system architectures. In their practice, agents typically use about four times more tokens than simple chat interactions, representing a baseline increase. However, multi-agent systems use about fifteen times more tokens than standard chat interactions due to the parallel operation of multiple subagents with separate context windows. This high token consumption means that multi-agent systems require tasks where the value of the task is high enough to pay for the increased performance. The economic viability of multi-agent systems depends on the high-value nature of tasks involving heavy parallelization.
questions.question: According to the content, what is the approximate token usage ratio of multi-agent systems compared to standard chat interactions?
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats, which is the correct ratio to distinguish from the baseline agent usage of 4× more tokens.

questions.lessonTitle: Production Engineering and Reliability: Error Recovery Process
questions.lessonContent: In multi-agent systems, reliability requires careful engineering of error handling and recovery mechanisms. Since agents can run for long periods maintaining state, we need to durably execute code and handle errors along the way. Without effective mitigations, minor system failures can be catastrophic for agents. When errors occur, we can't just restart from the beginning: restarts are expensive and frustrating for users. Instead, we built systems that can resume from where the agent was when the errors occurred. We also use the model's intelligence to handle issues gracefully—for instance, letting the agent know when a tool is failing and letting it adapt works surprisingly well.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in Anthropic's error recovery process for multi-agent systems?

questions.lessonTitle: Base Model Selection for Continued Pretraining
questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage uses a selected base model to improve the language model's base knowledge, specifically in the domain of coding. The researchers used internal evaluations and inference performance considerations to select a base model. Their evaluations measured internal codebase perplexity, coding knowledge, and state tracking. These evaluations led them to select Kimi K2.5 as the base model for Composer 2. Kimi K2.5 is a 1.04T parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 32B active parameters.
questions.question: What is the name of the base model selected for Composer 2 continued pretraining?

questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage is divided into three distinct phases. The first phase involves spending the bulk of compute at 32k token sequence length. The second phase is a shorter long-context extension phase that extends the sequence length to 256k tokens. The third phase is a short supervised fine-tuning phase focused on targeted coding tasks. This staged approach progressively filters towards higher quality data and specializes the model on coding knowledge and capabilities.
questions.question: Continued pretraining uses three phases: bulk training at 32k tokens, followed by long-context extension to 256k tokens, and finally a short SFT phase on targeted coding tasks.

questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage aims to improve the language model's base knowledge specifically in the domain of coding. Such continued pretraining has long been demonstrated to drastically improve downstream performance. While the model starts with base models naturally trained with large amounts of code data, the researchers find that additional supervised learning reliably improves knowledge benchmarks and leads to improved coding performance of the final coding agent. The purpose is to provide a base model for the subsequent agentic RL training by specializing the model on coding knowledge and capabilities.
questions.question: What is the primary purpose of the continued pretraining stage in Composer 2 training?
choices: To perform large-scale reinforcement learning to improve end-to-end coding performance
To develop infrastructure for training in the same Cursor harness used by the deployed model
To evaluate the model on CursorBench and public software engineering benchmarks
To specialize the model on coding knowledge and provide a base model for subsequent agentic RL training
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that the purpose of continued pretraining is to 'provide a base model for the subsequent agentic RL training by specializing the model on coding knowledge and capabilities.' The other options describe RL training, evaluation, or infrastructure development, which are separate from continued pretraining.

questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage for Composer 2 follows a structured three-phase approach. First, the bulk of compute is spent at 32k token sequence length to improve the model's base coding knowledge. Second, a shorter long-context extension phase extends the sequence length to 256k tokens. Third, a brief supervised fine-tuning phase focuses on targeted coding tasks. During this process, Multi-Token Prediction layers are initialized from scratch, trained with self-distillation to predict exact logit distributions, and finally included in joint training during the last two phases.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Composer 2 continued pretraining pipeline?

questions.lessonContent: To enable Composer 2 to work across long horizons, the training uses the self-summarization technique introduced in Composer 1.5. Each training rollout can involve multiple generations chained together by summaries, rather than a single prompt-response pair. The training uses the final reward for all tokens produced by the model in the chain. This approach upweights both the agent responses in good trajectories and also the self-summarizations that made them work. At the same time, poor summaries that lose critical information are downweighted. As Composer trains, it learns to use self-summaries to process more information, even with a limited context window.
questions.question: In self-summarization, how is reward applied to the tokens produced by the model in a chained rollout?
questions.answer: The final reward is applied to all tokens produced by the model in the chain

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2's reinforcement learning pipeline is built around learning from large-scale policy gradients while maintaining stability. The training uses a policy gradient algorithm with multiple samples per prompt and a fixed group size. They operate in the single-epoch regime, meaning the same prompt is never trained on twice. The underlying optimizer used is Adam, and the full parameter set is updated. RL training operates in a highly asynchronous regime with independent training and rollout generation workers.
questions.question: Composer 2 uses a policy gradient algorithm that operates in the single-epoch regime, meaning the same prompt is never trained on twice.

questions.lessonContent: While the primary goal of RL training is to improve model intelligence, the training also aims to produce a model that provides a good developer experience. This is affected by the communication style of the model as well as the time and resources it takes to answer a question. For behavior and communication, the training applies an array of auxiliary rewards to ensure the model provides a good experience. These auxiliary rewards include rewards for coding style, communication, and product-specific penalties for poor tool calls such as creating to-do list items and then leaving them unfinished. During RL training, the model is monitored for emergent behaviors and occasionally additional behavior rewards are introduced as needed.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a type of auxiliary reward applied during Composer 2's RL training for agent behavior?
choices: Product-specific penalties for poor tool calls
questions.explanation: The content explicitly mentions rewards for coding style, rewards for communication, and product-specific penalties for poor tool calls. Rewards for code execution speed is not mentioned as an auxiliary reward type.

questions.lessonContent: The agent behavior shaping process in Composer 2 RL training involves multiple stages. First, we apply an array of auxiliary rewards to ensure the model provides a good developer experience, including rewards for coding style, communication, and product-specific penalties. During RL training, we actively monitor the model for emergent behaviors that may need addressing. Based on these observations, we occasionally introduce additional behavior rewards as needed—for example, when we noticed the model would start to leave long chains-of-thought in comments or collapse to using the terminal tool only. This systematic approach of applying rewards, monitoring outcomes, and introducing corrections ultimately produces the desired shaped agent behavior.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the agent behavior shaping process for Composer 2 RL training?

questions.lessonContent: Public evaluation benchmarks often correlate only loosely with the real-world utility of coding models due to four primary factors. First, Domain Mismatch occurs because static benchmarks fail to capture the full spectrum of developer workflows as coding agent capabilities expand. Second, Prompt Over-specification happens when public benchmarks are highly specified with narrow sets of correct solutions, while real developer requests are often under-specified and admit multiple valid approaches. Third, Data Contamination and Overfitting arises because public benchmarks constructed from historical open-source repository scrapes are frequently leaked into model training mixtures. Fourth, Narrow Evaluation Scope means existing coding evaluations predominantly measure functional correctness while developers heavily weigh code quality, readability, latency, cost, and interactive agent behavior.
questions.question: What are the four primary factors that cause public evaluation benchmarks to correlate only loosely with the real-world utility of coding models?
questions.answer: Domain Mismatch, Prompt Over-specification, Data Contamination and Overfitting, and Narrow Evaluation Scope

questions.lessonTitle: Precision Format Usage in Composer 2 Training
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 training uses both MXFP8 and NVFP4 precision formats for the Mixture-of-Experts layer. For the MoE forward pass, a novel variant of NVFP4 is used where values are quantized from BF16 into FP4E2M1 using FP8E4M3 per-block scales with block size 16 and FP32 per-token scales. For the MoE backward pass, the standard MXFP8 format is used with FP8E4M3 values and FP8E8M0 scales per 32-element block. The forward pass uses NVFP4 specifically to match inference for numerical stability, while the backward pass can afford higher precision to improve training stability.
questions.question: In Composer 2's MoE training, the forward pass uses NVFP4 while the backward pass uses MXFP8.

questions.lessonContent: The RL infrastructure for Composer 2 consists of four decoupled services: training, environments, inference, and evaluations. This decoupled service stack enables larger-scale global training, high availability, and independent scaling and sharding. The training service uses a fully asynchronous, high-throughput stack built on Ray and PyTorch with a centralized reconciler for slot-based sample lifecycle state management. Environments run on Anyrun, an internal compute platform for running untrusted code at scale. Inference is partnered with Fireworks AI. Online evaluations use a pinned version of the production backend and Cursor client.
questions.question: How many decoupled services make up the RL infrastructure for Composer 2, and what are they?
choices: Three services: training, inference, and environments
Five services: training, environments, inference, evaluations, and monitoring
Four services: training, environments, inference, and evaluations
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states: 'Our RL infrastructure consists of four decoupled services: training, environments, inference, and evaluations.'

questions.lessonContent: The evaluation workflow involves initializing a codebase environment for each CursorBench task, then running the Cursor agent in that environment exactly as it would execute in production. Once the agent completes its rollout, we compute accuracy by checking whether the agent successfully solved the task. This process is repeated across multiple passes to reduce variance in the final scores.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the CursorBench evaluation process?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. You can place CLAUDE.md files in several locations including the root of your repo, any parent or child of the directory where you run claude, and your home folder. There are two naming conventions: CLAUDE.md which should be checked into git to share across sessions and with your team, and CLAUDE.local.md which should be .gitignored to keep personal settings private to your local environment.
questions.question: What is the filename for a CLAUDE.md file that should be gitignored?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. You can place CLAUDE.md files in several locations to customize your setup. The most common location is the root of your repo where you run claude from. Additionally, you can place CLAUDE.md in your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, which applies it to all your Claude sessions regardless of which directory you work in. This allows you to have global settings that persist across all projects.
questions.question: CLAUDE.md files can be placed in your home folder to apply to all Claude Code sessions.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation, making it ideal for documenting bash commands, code style guidelines, testing instructions, repository etiquette, and developer environment setup. You can place CLAUDE.md files in multiple locations to control their scope. The most common placement is the root of your repo where you run claude from. For monorepos, you can place CLAUDE.md in any parent directory of where you run claude, and Claude will pull in files from both the parent and child directories. You can also place CLAUDE.md in your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md to apply settings globally across all projects.
questions.question: Which of the following is a valid location for placing a CLAUDE.md file?
choices: Only the root of your repository
Only in the current working directory
The root of your repo, or anywhere you run claude from
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states CLAUDE.md files can be placed in several locations: the root of your repo (the most common usage), any parent of the directory where you run claude, any child of the directory where you run claude, and your home folder (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md).

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: When customizing Claude Code, the first step involves creating the CLAUDE.md file which serves as a special file automatically pulled into context during conversations. After creating the file, you should add project context to file by documenting common bash commands, code style guidelines, testing instructions, and other relevant project information. Finally, you tune CLAUDE.md instructions by experimenting with the content and refining it like any frequently used prompt to ensure optimal instruction following from the model.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in customizing Claude Code setup?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Extending Claude with Tools and Workflows
questions.lessonContent: Custom slash commands are stored as Markdown files within the .claude/commands folder in your project directory. These command templates become available through the slash commands menu when you type the / character in Claude Code. The special keyword $ARGUMENTS can be included in custom slash commands to pass parameters from the command invocation. For example, putting content into .claude/commands/fix-github-issue.md makes it available as /project:fix-github-issue. Personal commands can also be added to ~/.claude/commands for availability across all sessions.

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code includes headless mode for non-interactive contexts like CI, pre-commit hooks, build scripts, and automation. Headless mode is triggered using the -p flag with a prompt, and the --output-format stream-json flag enables streaming JSON output. questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Extending Claude with Tools and Workflows
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code can connect to MCP servers to access their tools in three distinct ways. First, MCP servers can be configured in project config, making them available when running Claude Code in that specific directory. Second, they can be added to global config, making them available across all projects. Third, they can be checked into a .mcp.json file, which makes them available to anyone working in the codebase. For example, adding Puppeteer and Sentry servers to your .mcp.json makes them available to every engineer working on your repository out of the box.

choices: Adding them to the CLAUDE.md file
questions.explanation: MCP servers can be checked into a .mcp.json file, which makes them available to anyone working in the codebase, such as every engineer on a repository.
