For images with lots of similar regions like solid backgrounds or gradients, this technique significantly reduces file size. This is the same algorithm used by ZIP files.
questions.question: LZ77 maintains a sliding window of the last ____ KB of data when searching for repeated patterns.

questions.lessonContent: After filtering and pattern-finding, some values appear more often than others in the compressed data. The value 0 (representing no difference) might appear 60% of the time, while 127 might appear only 5%. Huffman coding gives common values shorter binary codes: 0 (appears 60%) gets just 1 bit, 2 (appears 25%) gets 2 bits, 255 (appears 10%) gets 3 bits, and 127 (appears 5%) gets 3 bits. This is similar to Morse code where the common letter "E" is just a dot while rare letters like "Q" are longer dashes. The math works out to 5x smaller: 60×1 + 25×2 + 10×3 + 5×3 = 155 bits instead of 100×8 = 800 bits.
questions.question: According to the source, the value 0 (appearing 60% of the time) receives how many bits in Huffman coding?

questions.lessonContent: In lossless compression, after applying filters to predict pixel values from neighbors, the algorithm scans the filtered data to identify repeated sequences. When LZ77 runs, it examines a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data to find these repeated patterns. Once found, the algorithm replaces the second occurrence with a compact back-reference that specifies how far back to look and how many bytes to copy. This three-step sequence of finding patterns, running LZ77, and replacing with references significantly reduces file size for images with similar regions.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the LZ77 pattern replacement process?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Roman Empire existed in two distinct historical periods. The first period was the Roman Republic, which lasted from 509 BCE to 30 BCE. The second period was the Roman Empire, which lasted from 30 BCE to 476 CE. It is important to note that Rome technically had an empire during the Roman Republic as well, but the term 'Roman Empire' specifically refers to the time period beginning with Augustus when Rome was ruled by emperors.
questions.question: What are the dates for the Roman Republic and the Roman Empire?
questions.answer: Roman Republic: 509 BCE-30 BCE; Roman Empire: 30 BCE-476 CE

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Latin phrase primus inter pares translates to 'first among equals.' Augustus and later emperors tried to maintain the façade that they were elected officials rather than dictators. Being 'first among equals' gave the illusion that an emperor was the most prestigious and important member of the Roman Senate, but that each senator was simultaneously equally important. In reality, the Roman emperors ruled with little input from anyone else, despite this pretense of equality.
questions.question: The phrase primus inter pares describes an emperor as being the first among equals with the senators.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium, becoming sole ruler of Rome. The Senate gave him the name 'Augustus,' meaning 'most high.' In 23 BCE, he was made consul for life and also given the titles 'Princeps' (first citizen), 'Imperator' (successful general), 'Pontifex Maximus' (chief religious leader), and tribunician power. Augustus built and maintained the empire's infrastructure including roads, established fire and police departments for Rome, and extended citizenship to more and more provincials. He famously said he 'found Rome a city of bricks and left it a city of marble.'
questions.question: Which of the following titles was given to Octavian (Augustus) by the Senate?
questions.explanation: The Senate gave Augustus the titles 'Princeps,' 'Imperator,' and 'Pontifex Maximus.' The title 'Censor' was not among those given.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: Module 1: The Rise of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: After defeating Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium, Octavian became the sole ruler of Rome. The Senate then gave him the name Augustus, meaning "most high." Finally, in 23 BCE, Octavian (now Augustus) was made consul for life by the Senate.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in Octavian's rise to power?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Roman Emperors and Imperial Rule
questions.lessonContent: In 23 BCE, the Senate made Octavian (now referred to as Augustus) consul for life. They also gave him the title "Princeps," meaning "first citizen," which became the origin of the word "prince." Alongside this title, Augustus was also given "Imperator" (origin of the word "emperor"), "Pontifex Maximus" (origin of the word "pontiff"), and the powers to call the Senate, veto laws, and make laws himself. Despite holding these powers, Augustus and later emperors tried to maintain the façade that they were elected officials rather than dictators.
questions.question: What title did Augustus receive that means "first citizen"?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Roman Emperors and Imperial Rule
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Claudius brought southern Britannia (what later became Great Britain) under Roman control during his reign from 41-54 CE. He also brought several kingdoms in the East under Roman influence. Claudius became emperor because he was the last adult male of his family, being the brother of Germanicus and uncle of Caligula. He conducted a census of the empire in 48 CE and opened the Senate up to provincials, allowing people from the provinces to serve as senators.
questions.question: Claudius successfully brought southern Britannia under Roman control.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Roman Emperors and Imperial Rule
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Diocletian believed that dividing the empire for administrative purposes would strengthen it. In 285 CE, he divided the empire into two administrative realms: the Eastern (Byzantine) Empire and the Western (Roman) Empire. This was the first step in creating what would become two separate empires. However, once Constantine established Constantinople as a capital city, the east-west split deepened, ultimately leading to the permanent division of the Roman world.
questions.question: Who divided the Roman Empire into two administrative realms in 285 CE?
questions.explanation: Diocletian was the emperor who divided the empire into Eastern and Western administrative realms in 285 CE, believing it would strengthen administration.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Roman Emperors and Imperial Rule
questions.lessonContent: The Year of the Four Emperors (69 CE) was a brief period of civil war after the death of Emperor Nero. Four emperors ruled in quick succession during this chaotic time: first Nero dies by forced suicide, then Galba becomes emperor, followed by Otho who replaces Galba, then Vitellius defeats Otho, and finally Vespasian defeats Vitellius to establish the new Flavian dynasty.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Year of the Four Emperors?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall and Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonTitle: The Fall of the Western Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Western Roman Empire ended officially in 476 CE when the last emperor, Romulus Augustus, was deposed by a barbarian named Odoacer. This event marks the traditional date for the fall of the Western Roman Empire. The Eastern (Byzantine) Empire lasted much longer, continuing until 1453 when it was conquered by the Ottoman Turks. The empire had gradually weakened over centuries due to a combination of economic, military, political, and social factors that accumulated over time.
questions.question: In what year did the Western Roman Empire officially end?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall and Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonContent: Constantine was the first Roman emperor to convert to Christianity, doing so on his deathbed in 337 CE. His mother Helena had already converted to Christianity before him. Constantine's conversion was significant because it led to Christianity gaining acceptance in the Roman Empire. Prior to this, the Edict of Milan in 313 CE had legalized Christianity and granted religious toleration throughout the empire. Future Roman emperors were Christians, and Christianity eventually became the official religion of the Roman Empire.
questions.question: Constantine converted to Christianity before becoming emperor.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Fall and Legacy of Rome
questions.lessonContent: The fall of the Western Roman Empire was caused by multiple interrelated factors. Economically, there was a growing gap between rich and poor, and impoverished workers became tied to the land as coloni who were sold with the land. As fewer people could afford to buy goods, manufacturing and trade declined. Militarily, armies made and unmade emperors rather than serving Rome, and reliance on barbarian troops who were not ultimately loyal created problems. Politically, there was no orderly succession, with murders, forced suicides, and civil wars frequently accompanying transitions between emperors. Socially, population decline from hunger, plagues, and war weakened the empire.
questions.question: Which of the following was NOT mentioned as an economic reason for the fall of Rome?
choices: Impoverished workers tied to the land as coloni
questions.explanation: Overreliance on barbarian troops was listed as a military reason for Rome's fall, not an economic reason. The economic reasons included the gap between rich and poor, workers becoming tied to the land as coloni, and the decline in manufacturing and trade due to lack of purchasing power.

results.file: How we built our multi-agent research system _ Anthropic.pdf

questions.lessonTitle: Understanding Multi-Agent Systems Definition and Core Benefits
questions.lessonContent: A multi-agent system consists of multiple agents, defined as LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop, working together to accomplish complex tasks. Research work involves open-ended problems where it is very difficult to predict the required steps in advance, making AI agents particularly well-suited for these tasks due to their need for flexibility to pivot or explore tangential connections as investigations unfold. The essence of search is compression: distilling insights from a vast corpus, and subagents facilitate this compression by operating in parallel with their own context windows, exploring different aspects of a question simultaneously before condensing the most important tokens for the lead research agent. Multi-agent systems become a vital way to scale performance once intelligence reaches a threshold, as groups of agents can accomplish far more than individuals. These systems excel especially for breadth-first queries that involve pursuing multiple independent directions simultaneously.
questions.question: According to the content, what is a multi-agent system?
questions.answer: A multi-agent system consists of multiple agents (LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop) working together

questions.lessonTitle: Performance Advantages of Multi-Agent Research Systems
questions.lessonContent: Internal evaluations by the organization show that multi-agent research systems excel particularly for breadth-first queries involving multiple independent directions. Their multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on their internal research eval. For example, when asked to identify all board members of companies in the Information Technology S&P 500, the multi-agent system found correct answers by decomposing this into tasks for subagents, while the single agent system failed with slow, sequential searches. In their analysis of the BrowseComp evaluation, three factors explained 95% of the performance variance, with token usage alone explaining 80% of the variance, while the number of tool calls and model choice were the two other explanatory factors.
questions.question: A multi-agent research system with Claude Opus 4 as lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperforms single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on internal research evaluation.

questions.lessonContent: The Research system uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously. The subagents act as intelligent filters by iteratively using search tools to gather information and then returning findings to the lead agent so it can compile a final answer. The architecture uses multi-step search that dynamically finds relevant information, adapts to new findings, and analyzes results to formulate high-quality answers, contrasting with traditional Retrieval Augmented Generation approaches that use static retrieval. This architecture distributes work across agents with separate context windows to add more capacity for parallel reasoning.
questions.question: What architecture pattern does the Research system use for its multi-agent system?
choices: Parallel independent agents with no central coordination
Orchestrator-worker pattern where a lead agent coordinates specialized subagents
Single-agent pipeline with sequential tool calls
Hierarchical agent chain with one parent directing all children
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states the Research system uses 'a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel.'

questions.moduleTitle: Architectural Design, Prompt Engineering, and Evaluation
questions.lessonTitle: Orchestrator-Worker Pattern in Multi-Agent Research Systems
questions.lessonContent: The Research system uses an orchestrator-worker pattern for its multi-agent architecture. A lead agent acts as the orchestrator, analyzing user queries, developing research strategies, and spawning specialized subagents to explore different aspects of a topic simultaneously. Each subagent operates independently with its own context window, using search tools to gather information before returning findings to the lead agent. The lead agent then synthesizes these results and decides whether additional research is needed. This architecture allows the system to handle complex, open-ended research tasks that require exploring multiple directions in parallel.
questions.question: What architectural pattern does the Research system use for coordinating multiple agents?

questions.moduleTitle: Architectural Design, Prompt Engineering, and Evaluation
questions.lessonTitle: Prompt Engineering Requires Scaling Effort to Query Complexity
questions.lessonContent: Multi-agent systems require careful prompt engineering to allocate resources appropriately. Anthropic embedded scaling rules in their prompts to help agents judge appropriate effort for different tasks. Simple fact-finding queries require just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls, while direct comparisons might need 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each. Complex research tasks may use more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities. These explicit guidelines help the lead agent allocate resources efficiently and prevent overinvestment in simple queries, which was a common failure mode in early versions of their system.
questions.question: According to the content, embedding scaling rules in prompts helps prevent overinvestment in simple queries, which was a common failure mode in early multi-agent systems.

questions.moduleTitle: Architectural Design, Prompt Engineering, and Evaluation
questions.lessonTitle: Evaluation Criteria for Multi-Agent Research Systems
questions.lessonContent: Evaluating multi-agent research systems requires flexible methods that assess outcomes rather than rigid adherence to prescribed steps. Anthropic used an LLM judge to evaluate outputs against criteria including factual accuracy (whether claims match sources), citation accuracy (whether cited sources match claims), completeness (whether all requested aspects are covered), source quality (whether primary sources were preferred over lower-quality secondary sources), and tool efficiency (whether the right tools were used a reasonable number of times). They found that a single LLM call with a prompt outputting scores from 0.0-1.0 and a pass-fail grade was most consistent and aligned with human judgments.
questions.question: Which of the following IS one of the evaluation criteria used by Anthropic's LLM judge for assessing research outputs?
questions.explanation: The LLM judge evaluates factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, and tool efficiency. All four options except 'Response creativity score' are mentioned in the content as evaluation criteria.

questions.moduleTitle: Architectural Design, Prompt Engineering, and Evaluation
questions.lessonContent: In the multi-agent research system, once a LeadResearcher creates specialized subagents with specific research tasks, each subagent independently performs web searches and evaluates tool results. After the subagents complete their searches, the LeadResearcher synthesizes these results to compile findings. This process allows for parallel exploration of different aspects of a query before consolidating the information.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the multi-agent research workflow?

questions.lessonContent: Agent systems are highly stateful webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously. This means that whenever Anthropic deploys updates, agents might be anywhere in their process. They need to prevent well-meaning code changes from breaking existing agents. They cannot update every agent to the new version at the same time. Instead, Anthropic uses rainbow deployments to avoid disrupting running agents, by gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously.
questions.question: What deployment technique does Anthropic use to prevent code updates from disrupting agents that are already running?

questions.lessonContent: Anthropic's lead agents currently execute subagents synchronously, waiting for each set of subagents to complete before proceeding. This simplifies coordination but creates bottlenecks in the information flow between agents. With synchronous execution, the lead agent cannot steer subagents, subagents cannot coordinate with each other, and the entire system can be blocked while waiting for a single subagent to finish searching.
questions.question: According to the content, Anthropic's lead agents execute subagents synchronously, waiting for each set to complete before proceeding, which creates bottlenecks in information flow.

questions.lessonContent: Agents can run for long periods of time, maintaining state across many tool calls. This means errors can compound significantly over time. Without effective mitigations, minor system failures can be catastrophic for agents. When errors occur, restarting from the beginning is expensive and frustrating for users. Anthropic builds systems that can resume from where the agent was when the errors occurred, combining the adaptability of AI agents built on Claude with deterministic safeguards like retry logic and regular checkpoints.
questions.question: Which approach does Anthropic use to handle errors in long-running agent systems without requiring expensive restarts from the beginning?
choices: Automatically terminating and restarting the agent from the initial state
Building systems that can resume from where the agent was when errors occurred
Relying solely on the model to handle all error recovery without additional safeguards
Using only deterministic safeguards like retry logic without checkpoint systems
questions.explanation: Anthropic builds systems that can resume from where the agent was when errors occurred, combining AI adaptability with deterministic safeguards like retry logic and regular checkpoints.

questions.lessonTitle: Production Reliability: Agent Error Recovery Process
questions.lessonContent: In the Production reliability and engineering challenges section, the text describes how agents handle errors durably. When errors occur in an agent running for long periods, the system cannot simply restart from the beginning as restarts are expensive and frustrating for users. Instead, the system builds resilience by combining deterministic safeguards like retry logic and regular checkpoints with the model's intelligence to handle issues gracefully. When errors occur, the system can resume from where the agent was at the last checkpoint, the retry logic executes to attempt recovery, and the agent adapts to the issue to complete the task successfully.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the agent error recovery process?

questions.moduleTitle: Introduction to Composer 2 and Foundation Concepts
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is a specialized model designed specifically for agentic software engineering. The model demonstrates strong long-term planning and coding intelligence while maintaining the ability to efficiently solve problems for interactive use. It is trained in two distinct phases: first, continued pretraining to improve the model’s knowledge and latent coding ability, followed by large-scale reinforcement learning to improve end-to-end coding performance through stronger reasoning, accurate multi-step execution, and coherence on long-horizon realistic coding problems. A core tenet of Composer training is to emulate real-world user challenges as closely as possible to minimize train-test mismatch.
questions.question: What is the primary design purpose of Composer 2?

questions.moduleTitle: Introduction to Composer 2 and Foundation Concepts
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is trained using infrastructure that supports training in the same Cursor harness that is used by the deployed model, with equivalent tools and structure. The environments used in training match real problems closely. This approach is designed to minimize train-test mismatch by emulating real-world user challenges as closely as possible. To measure the ability of the model on increasingly difficult tasks, the team introduces a benchmark derived from real software engineering problems in large codebases including their own.
questions.question: Composer 2 uses identical infrastructure to the production Cursor harness during training, with equivalent tools and structure. True or false?

questions.moduleTitle: Introduction to Composer 2 and Foundation Concepts
questions.lessonContent: The evaluations for base model selection measured internal codebase perplexity, coding knowledge, and state tracking. These evaluations led to the selection of Kimi K2.5 as the base model for Composer 2. Kimi K2.5 is a 1.04T parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 32B active parameters. This model was chosen after evaluating several potential open-source base models including GLM-5, Kimi K2.5, and DeepSeek V3.2.
questions.question: Which base model was selected for Composer 2 and what are its parameter specifications?
choices: GLM-5 with 1.04T total parameters and 32B active parameters
DeepSeek V3.2 with 1.04T total parameters and 32B active parameters
Kimi K2.5 with 1.04T total parameters and 32B active parameters
Qwen3-Coder-30B with 1.04T total parameters and 32B active parameters
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that evaluations led to selecting Kimi K2.5 as the base model, which is a 1.04T parameter / 32B active parameter Mixture-of-Experts model.

questions.moduleTitle: Introduction to Composer 2 and Foundation Concepts
questions.lessonContent: The Composer 2 training process begins with continued pretraining on a large code-dominated data mix to improve the model's base knowledge in coding. This is followed by a long-context extension phase that increases the sequence length from 32k to 256k tokens. Finally, a short SFT phase on targeted coding tasks completes the preparation before reinforcement learning.
questions.question: What is the correct order of the initial training phases in Composer 2's continued pretraining stage?

questions.moduleTitle: Training Methodology: Continued Pretraining and Reinforcement Learning
questions.lessonTitle: Continued Pretraining Improves Downstream RL Performance
questions.lessonContent: The connection between continued pretraining and downstream RL performance is an area of active research. The relationship between codebase perplexity and RL performance was studied by applying the continued pretraining recipe to Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B. Continued pretraining was performed at three logarithmically spaced compute levels: small, medium, and large. Each checkpoint then underwent SFT on a small dataset, followed by an identical RL run. The study demonstrated that cross-entropy loss after SFT is indeed predictive of downstream RL performance, showing that continued pretraining serves to improve the model's latent coding ability which translates to better RL outcomes.
questions.question: What did the relationship study between codebase perplexity and RL performance demonstrate?
questions.answer: Cross-entropy loss is predictive of downstream RL performance

questions.moduleTitle: Training Methodology: Continued Pretraining and Reinforcement Learning
questions.lessonTitle: Nonlinear Length Penalty in RL Training
questions.lessonContent: To incentivize the model to produce solutions quickly on easy requests while allowing it to think longer on hard requests, a concave down and increasing nonlinear length penalty is added to the reward. The formula is Clength{k,q}(x) = ((1 + kx)^(1-q) - 1) / (k(1-q)), where k and q are hyperparameters which define the curvature of the penalty, and the input x is a weighted combination of thinking tokens, tool calling tokens, tool output tokens, final message tokens, number of tool calls, and number of turns of a rollout. The nonlinearity reflects that on easy tasks, achievable with only a few tool calls, every additional bit of effort is felt more acutely than in long-horizon tasks, where the agent might iterate for hundreds of tool calls. This length penalty enables the model to learn particularly efficient behaviors, such as making multiple tool calls in parallel.
questions.question: What does the nonlinear length penalty formula use as input x?
choices: The sum of thinking tokens and final message tokens only
Only the number of tool calls and total token count
The length of the response in characters only
A weighted combination of thinking tokens, tool calling tokens, tool output tokens, final message tokens, number of tool calls, and number of turns of a rollout
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that x is 'a weighted combination of thinking tokens, tool calling tokens, tool output tokens, final message tokens, number of tool calls, and number of turns of a rollout'.

questions.moduleTitle: Training Methodology: Continued Pretraining and Reinforcement Learning
questions.lessonContent: In Composer 2's reinforcement learning training, the process begins by selecting a coding task from the problem distribution, then the model generates multiple solution attempts through rollouts, and finally the advantages are computed to measure solution quality relative to other attempts in the group.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in Composer 2's reinforcement learning training pipeline?

questions.lessonContent: CursorBench represents a more realistic evaluation of software engineering capabilities compared to public benchmarks. The tasks require substantially more extensive code modifications, with a median of 181 lines changed compared to just 7-10 lines for SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. Additionally, CursorBench prompts are more under-specified, featuring a median description length of only 390 characters versus 1,185-3,055 characters for public benchmarks. This combination of broad execution scope and high intent ambiguity accurately reflects the intrinsic difficulty of real-world software engineering.
questions.question: What is the median number of lines changed in CursorBench tasks?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 was evaluated on CursorBench-3, achieving 61.3% accuracy. This represents a 37% relative improvement over Composer 1.5 (which achieved 44.2%) and a 61% improvement over Composer 1 (which achieved 38.0%). These evaluations were conducted by running Cursor agents directly within Anyrun, the same infrastructure that supports the reinforcement learning pipeline. For each task, the codebase environment was initialized with the initial task prompt, and the agent executed exactly as it would in the production environment.
questions.question: Composer 2 achieves 61.3% on CursorBench, representing a 37% relative improvement over Composer 1.5. True or false?

questions.lessonContent: The RL infrastructure for Composer 2 consists of four decoupled services: training, environments, inference, and evaluations. This decoupled service architecture enables larger-scale global training, high availability, and independent scaling and sharding. The production training job for Composer 2 spanned 3 regions for GPU compute and 4 regions for CPU compute. Within the Anyrun environment infrastructure, each cluster is capable of scheduling more than 500 pods per second while maintaining desired binpacking requirements, with each pod being a dedicated Firecracker VM capable of running a full development environment.
questions.question: How many regions were used for GPU compute and CPU compute respectively in Composer 2's production training job?
questions.explanation: The production training job for Composer 2 spanned 3 regions for GPU compute and 4 regions for CPU compute.

questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. You can place CLAUDE.md files in several locations: the root of your repo (where you run claude), any parent of the directory where you run claude (useful for monorepos), any child of the directory where you run claude (files pulled on demand), and your home folder (~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) which applies to all sessions. The recommended naming is CLAUDE.md to check into git for sharing across sessions and teams. Alternatively, you can name it CLAUDE.local.md and .gitignore it for personal preferences.
questions.question: What is the recommended naming for a CLAUDE.md file that should be checked into git for team sharing?

questions.lessonTitle: CLAUDE.md File Placement in Directory Hierarchy
questions.lessonContent: Claude automatically pulls CLAUDE.md files into context based on the directory where you run the claude command. Specifically, it pulls files from parent directories of where you run claude, allowing nested contexts in monorepo structures, and from child directories when you work with files in those child directories.
questions.question: When running Claude from a subdirectory in a monorepo, CLAUDE.md files in parent directories of that subdirectory will be automatically pulled into context.

questions.lessonTitle: Methods for Managing Allowed Tools in Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code has a deliberately conservative approach to tool permissions for safety. There are four ways to manage the allowlist of tools: select "Always allow" when prompted during a session, use the /permissions command after starting Claude Code to add or remove tools, manually edit your .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json files, or use the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions. The /permissions command allows adding tools like Edit, Bash(git commit:*), or MCP tools such as mcp__puppeteer__puppeteer_navigate.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a method for managing allowed tools in Claude Code?
choices: Using the /config command to modify tool permissions
Using the /permissions command to add or remove tools
Selecting "Always allow" when prompted during a session
questions.explanation: The /permissions command is used to manage allowed tools, not /config. The other three options are valid methods: selecting "Always allow" when prompted, using /permissions command, and manually editing settings.json files.

questions.lessonContent: When setting up Claude Code for your project, you first need to create a CLAUDE.md file to define project-specific context. Once created, you must place it in the appropriate repository location where Claude will automatically detect it. After placement, you should tune your CLAUDE.md content by refining and iterating on its instructions to ensure optimal instruction following from the model.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in setting up CLAUDE.md for your repository?

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code can connect to MCP servers in three distinct ways to access their tools. First, you can configure MCP servers in your project config, which makes them available when running Claude Code in that specific directory. Second, MCP servers can be set in global config to make them available across all projects. Third, you can check in a .mcp.json file into your repository, which makes the MCP servers available to anyone working on your codebase without individual setup. For example, adding Puppeteer and Sentry servers to your .mcp.json allows every engineer on your repo to use these tools out of the box.
questions.question: In how many different ways can you configure MCP servers in Claude Code?

questions.lessonContent: When asking Claude to plan solutions, the specific word choice matters for triggering extended thinking mode. The content states that phrases like "think", "think hard", "think harder", and "ultrathink" are mapped directly to increasing levels of thinking budget in the system. Each level allocates progressively more thinking budget for Claude to use, allowing it to evaluate alternatives more thoroughly when solving complex problems.
questions.question: True or False: Using the phrase "ultrathink" gives Claude more thinking budget than using "think hard".

questions.lessonContent: Custom slash commands in Claude Code are stored as Markdown files in the .claude/commands folder and become available through the slash commands menu when you type /. These commands can be checked into git to share with your team. The custom slash commands can include the special keyword $ARGUMENTS to pass parameters from command invocation. For example, a command file containing 'Please analyze and fix the GitHub issue: $ARGUMENTS' would be invoked as /project:fix-github-issue 1234 to fix issue number 1234.
questions.question: What keyword allows custom slash commands to accept parameters from command invocation?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that custom slash commands can include the special keyword $ARGUMENTS to pass parameters from command invocation.

questions.lessonContent: The 'Explore, plan, code, commit' workflow is a versatile pattern for using Claude Code effectively. First, you should ask Claude to read relevant files, images, or URLs, providing general pointers or specific filenames, but explicitly telling it not to write any code just yet. Second, ask Claude to make a plan for how to approach the specific problem, and consider using the word 'think' to trigger extended thinking mode for more thorough evaluation. Third, ask Claude to implement its solution in code, and have it verify the reasonableness of its solution as it implements pieces. This workflow prevents Claude from jumping straight to coding without proper research and planning.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the 'Explore, plan, code, commit' workflow?

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code excels with images and diagrams through several methods. You can paste screenshots directly into the prompt input, which is particularly useful on macOS where you can hit cmd+ctrl+shift+4 to screenshot to clipboard and then ctrl+v to paste. You can also drag and drop images directly into the prompt input, or provide file paths for images. These capabilities are particularly useful when working with design mocks as reference points for UI development, and visual charts for analysis and debugging.
questions.question: What three methods does Claude Code support for receiving images?
questions.answer: Pasting screenshots, drag and drop, and providing file paths

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code includes headless mode for non-interactive contexts like CI, pre-commit hooks, build scripts, and automation. To enable headless mode, you use the -p flag with a prompt. For output formatting, you can use --output-format stream-json. It is important to note that headless mode does not persist between sessions, meaning you have to trigger it each session rather than having it carry over from a previous invocation.
questions.question: True or False: Headless mode in Claude Code persists between sessions automatically once enabled.

questions.lessonContent: Git worktrees allow you to check out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories. Each worktree has its own working directory with isolated files while sharing the same Git history and reflog. To create a worktree, you use the command 'git worktree add ../project-feature-a feature-a' where the first parameter specifies the directory path and the second specifies the branch name. After creating worktrees, you can launch Claude in each one by navigating to the directory and running the claude command.
questions.question: What is the correct git command syntax for creating a worktree?
questions.explanation: The correct syntax is 'git worktree add' followed by the directory path and branch name.

questions.lessonContent: The test-driven development (TDD) workflow for agentic coding involves writing tests first based on expected input/output pairs, then running them to confirm they fail before any implementation code exists. After committing the failing tests, Claude writes code to pass the tests without modifying them, iterating as needed until all tests pass. Finally, when satisfied with the implementation, the code is committed.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the test-driven development workflow?
choices: Write tests based on expected I/O
Write code that passes the tests
Run tests and confirm they fail

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint was released with 8 open source embedding models. These include top models from the MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark) leaderboard such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models. Additionally, the endpoint offers newly released M2-BERT retrieval models designed for long context applications. This variety allows users to choose the most appropriate model based on their specific use case and context length requirements.

The Together Embeddings endpoint was designed with full OpenAI API compatibility, allowing users who have already built applications following the OpenAI API to easily migrate their existing code. questions.question: The Together Embeddings endpoint has full OpenAI API compatibility, allowing easy migration for developers with existing OpenAI-based applications.
