questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the test-driven development workflow for writing tests?

questions.lessonContent: Text embeddings provide a measure of the similarity or relatedness of given text queries. This mathematical representation allows computers to understand the semantic relationship between different pieces of text. Embeddings are used for various applications including clustering, semantic search, and classification. Additionally, embeddings are essential for retrieval augmented generation (RAG), which aims to overcome limitations of generative AI models such as a lack of knowledge from unseen data.
questions.question: What do text embeddings provide a measure of?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint was released as a new product offering from Together AI. One of the key selling points of this endpoint is its pricing structure. According to the product announcement, users can access these powerful models at very competitive prices. The platform advertises that the Together Embeddings endpoint is up to 4 times cheaper than other popular platforms, making it an attractive option for developers and organizations looking to implement embedding-based solutions.

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint was launched with multiple open-source embedding models. According to the announcement, the platform offers 8 leading embedding models including models that outperform OpenAI's ada-002 and Cohere's Embed-v3 in MTEB and LoCo Benchmarks. The available models include top models from the MTEB leaderboard such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models, as well as the newly released M2-BERT retrieval models for long context which come in variants of 2k, 8k, and 32k context lengths.

questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that the Together Embeddings endpoint is available with 8 open source embeddings models, including top models from the MTEB leaderboard such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models, and the newly released M2-BERT retrieval models.

questions.lessonTitle: Configuring OpenAI-Compatible Client for Together Embeddings
questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint provides an OpenAI-compatible API to facilitate migration for developers who have already built applications using the OpenAI API. To use the Together endpoint, you must configure the OpenAI client with your Together API key and specify the base URL as "https://api.together.xyz/api/v1/embeddings". The model parameter should be set to one of the available embedding models, such as "togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-32k-retrieval" for long context retrieval. This configuration allows existing code to work with minimal changes by simply replacing the base URL and API key.

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint has been designed with full OpenAI compatibility to make migrating existing applications easier. This means developers who have already built applications following the OpenAI API can switch to the Together endpoint by simply changing the base URL and API key configuration. The client initialization uses the standard OpenAI library with the Together API key and base URL specified. This compatibility feature reduces the friction of switching providers and allows teams to leverage Together's pricing and model options without significant code refactoring.
questions.question: The Together Embeddings endpoint has full OpenAI API compatibility, allowing developers to migrate their existing applications with minimal code changes.

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint offers state-of-the-art M2-Retrieval models specifically designed for long context retrieval tasks. These models are available in three context length variants: 2k, 8k, and 32k, allowing users to handle very long documents without splitting them into many short chunks. The M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model (API string: togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-8k-retrieval) supports a context length of 8,000 tokens and produces embedding vectors with a dimension of 768. These long context models significantly outperform other closed models in retrieval tasks, enabling more meaningful contexts to be contained within the embeddings.
questions.question: What is the context length supported by the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model?
questions.explanation: The M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model (API string: togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-8k-retrieval) specifically supports an 8,000 token context length, as indicated by the '8k' in its name. The 32k variant is a separate model (togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-32k-retrieval).

questions.lessonTitle: API Client Setup and Embedding Request Workflow
questions.lessonContent: When using the Together Embeddings endpoint, the first step is to initialize the API client with your Together API key. Next, you configure model selection by specifying which embedding model you want to use, such as M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K. Finally, you create embeddings request by passing your input text through the client.embeddings.create() method to generate the embeddings.

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Applications and Data Visualization
questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint supports building Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) systems using the Together API. You can construct RAG applications by integrating with popular vector databases such as MongoDB, Pinecone, and Chroma. Additionally, the platform offers compatibility with established frameworks including LangChain and LlamaIndex. Detailed tutorials are available for building RAG using Together with MongoDB, using Together with LangChain, or using Together with LlamaIndex. To plot each data example in 2D, tSNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding) is used to transform the embedding vectors. questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Applications and Data Visualization

The function takes an embedding matrix with dimensions n by m (where n is the number of samples and m is the embedding dimension), along with n_components and perplexity parameters. The main script specifies n_components=2 to produce a 2D visualization and perplexity=15, which controls the balance of attention in tSNE between local and global aspects of the data. For the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model used in the example, the embedding dimension is 768. The visualization uses a color scheme with five colors (red, blue, green, orange, purple) to distinguish between different data sources.
questions.question: What n_components value is used in the main script for visualizing RedPajama-v1 sample data?

questions.lessonTitle: Building RAG Applications and Data Visualization

results.file: How does image compression work_ _ Lee Robinson.pdf

questions.lessonContent: Images look smooth and continuous, but when you zoom in far enough, you'll see they're made of tiny colored squares called pixels. Each pixel contains three numbers representing how much red, green, and blue to mix together to create the final color. Each of these color values ranges from 0, meaning none of that color, to 255, representing the maximum intensity of that color. For example, a pixel with rgb(255, 147, 41) would have maximum red, medium green, and low blue. This RGB system is the foundation for how digital images represent color.
questions.question: What are the three values that make up each pixel in a digital image?

questions.lessonTitle: Lossy Compression Cannot Restore Original Data
questions.lessonContent: There are two main approaches to image compression: lossy compression (used by JPEG) and lossless compression (used by PNG). Lossy compression exploits how human vision works by throwing away parts of the image that humans won't notice, such as high-frequency details. This approach can achieve 10-20x smaller files with minimal visible difference. However, with lossy compression, you cannot get the original pixels back once the data has been discarded. Lossless compression, on the other hand, preserves every single pixel while still shrinking the file size.
questions.question: With lossy compression, you can recover the original pixels after compression.

questions.lessonTitle: The Three Tricks of PNG Lossless Compression
questions.lessonContent: Lossless compression used by PNG preserves every single pixel while still shrinking file size using three main tricks. The first trick is filtering or prediction, where adjacent pixels are usually similar so instead of storing each value, the system stores how much each pixel differs from its neighbor. The second trick is LZ77, which finds repeated patterns in the data and replaces them with back-references, using a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data. The third trick is Huffman coding, which gives common values shorter binary codes—for instance, a value appearing 60% of the time might get just 1 bit while rare values get longer codes. For a photograph, these three tricks together can achieve 3x smaller file size, and for screenshots with large solid color regions, they can achieve 10-50x compression.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the three tricks used by PNG for lossless compression?
questions.explanation: The three tricks used by PNG are: 1) Filtering (or prediction), 2) LZ77 (finding patterns), and 3) Huffman coding (shorter codes for common values). Frequency transformation is used by JPEG, not PNG.

questions.lessonContent: PNG lossless compression uses three key techniques in sequence. First, filtering predicts each pixel's value from its neighbors to store differences instead of raw values. Second, LZ77 pattern finding scans for repeated sequences and replaces them with compact back-references. Third, Huffman coding assigns shorter binary codes to the most common values, similar to how Morse code uses shorter signals for frequent letters. These three steps work together to reduce file size while preserving every pixel perfectly.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the PNG lossless compression pipeline?

questions.lessonTitle: JPEG Block Size and Frequency Transformation
questions.lessonContent: JPEG compression uses a specific block-based approach to process images. First, it converts pixels from RGB to a different format that separates brightness from color. It also reduces color resolution since human eyes won't notice subtle color variations. Then, JPEG divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components. Low frequencies represent smooth gradients while high frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges.
questions.question: What is the block size used by JPEG for compression?

questions.lessonContent: Lossy compression exploits how human vision works to throw away data humans won't notice. Your eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together, so JPEG reduces color resolution since your eyes won't notice. It throws away high-frequency details like sharp edges while keeping smooth parts intact. This results in 10-20x smaller files with minimal visible difference. However, the original pixel data cannot be recovered after lossy compression.
questions.question: With lossy compression, you can recover the original pixels after compression.

questions.lessonContent: JPEG compression takes advantage of the fact that photographs are mostly smooth gradients with few sharp edges. When JPEG divides an image into 8×8 blocks and transforms them into frequency components, most of the information ends up in just a few low-frequency components. High frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges, which are less common in photographs. JPEG throws away the high-frequency details that human eyes won't miss, keeping only the low-frequency smooth parts that define the overall image appearance.
questions.question: For photographs, which frequency components does JPEG primarily keep?
questions.explanation: Photographs are mostly smooth gradients, so most information ends up in low-frequency components. JPEG keeps these while discarding high-frequency details.

questions.lessonContent: JPEG lossy compression works by first converting pixels from RGB to a different format that separates brightness from color. Then it divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components. This allows the algorithm to identify which details human vision is least likely to notice.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the JPEG lossy compression pipeline?

questions.lessonContent: LZ77 is a pattern-finding algorithm used in lossless compression. It maintains a sliding window of previously encoded data to find repeated patterns. According to the content, LZ77 maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data. Any pattern within that window can be referenced instead of repeated, allowing the encoder to say 'go back 5 values and copy 5' instead of storing the same sequence twice. For images with lots of similar regions like solid backgrounds or gradients, this technique helps reduce file size significantly.
questions.question: What is the size of the sliding window used by LZ77 for finding repeated patterns?

questions.lessonContent: Huffman coding is the third step in the PNG lossless compression pipeline. After filtering and pattern-finding, some values appear more often than others. Huffman coding gives common values shorter binary codes. For example, the value 0 (appearing 60% of the time) gets just 1 bit, while 127 (appearing only 5%) gets 3 bits. This same principle was used in Morse code, where common letters like E get shorter signals. The math works out to be approximately 5x smaller than storing all values with equal 8-bit codes.
questions.question: Huffman coding assigns shorter binary codes to values that appear more frequently in the compressed data.

questions.lessonContent: PNG files are organized into chunks, each with a specific purpose. The IHDR chunk is the image header and is required as the first chunk, containing essential metadata like width, height, bit depth, and color type. The IDAT chunk contains the actual compressed image data, and the IEND chunk marks the end of the PNG file. Each chunk includes a CRC-32 checksum at the end, which is a mathematical fingerprint used to detect if the file has become corrupted during transmission or storage.
questions.question: Which PNG chunk contains the image metadata including width, height, bit depth, and color type?
questions.explanation: The IHDR chunk is the required first chunk in a PNG file and contains image metadata such as width, height, bit depth, and color type.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Rise and Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Roman Empire existed from 30 BCE to 476 CE. This period began when Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium and became the sole ruler of Rome. The Senate gave Octavian the name Augustus, meaning 'most high.' The term 'Roman Empire' refers to the time period when Rome was ruled by emperors, beginning with Augustus.
questions.question: What are the start and end dates of the Roman Empire?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Rise and Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: Augustus and the Title Pontifex Maximus
questions.lessonContent: The Roman Senate gave Octavian multiple titles to reflect his power and authority. He was made 'Pontifex Maximus,' meaning 'chief religious leader.' This title is the origin of the word 'pontiff,' which is still used today to describe the pope. Augustus held this position as part of his consolidation of religious and political authority.
questions.question: Augustus was given the title Pontifex Maximus, meaning chief religious leader.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Rise and Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: In 23 BCE, the Senate made Octavian, now referred to as Augustus, consul for life. He was also made 'Princeps,' meaning 'first citizen.' This title is the origin of the word 'prince.' Augustus and later emperors used this title to maintain the illusion that they were elected officials rather than dictators, embodying the concept of being 'first among equals' in the Roman Senate.
questions.question: What does the title 'Princeps' mean, and from which Roman emperor did the word 'prince' originate?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is 'first citizen' because the content explicitly states that Augustus was made 'Princeps,' meaning 'first citizen,' and this is the origin of the word 'prince'.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Rise and Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: After defeating Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium, Octavian became the sole ruler of Rome. The Senate then gave him the name "Augustus," meaning "most high." Finally, in 23 BCE, Octavian, now referred to as Augustus, was made consul for life by the Senate.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in Augustus's rise to power?

questions.lessonContent: The Pax Romana, meaning Roman Peace, was a period of relative stability and prosperity throughout the Roman Empire. During this time, Rome controlled the entire Mediterranean region and beyond, achieving complete control that resulted in almost no warfare. This peace lasted nearly 200 years, beginning with Augustus's reign and continuing through the rule of several subsequent emperors. More and more provincials were granted official Roman citizenship during this period of unprecedented peace and expansion.
questions.question: What are the start and end dates of the Pax Romana?

questions.lessonContent: Gaius Augustus Germanicus, known as Caligula, was the son of the famed military leader Germanicus, who was the nephew and adopted son of Emperor Tiberius. Caligula earned his nickname 'Caligula,' meaning 'little boots,' from the Roman army as a child because he was dressed like a soldier. His reign began with two years of good and effective rule, but this was interrupted by a severe illness. Following his illness, Caligula's rule became horrible for two years, during which he exiled some family members, killed others, and forced additional perceived enemies to commit suicide. Caligula was assassinated in 41 CE by members of the Praetorian Guard.
questions.question: Caligula ruled for approximately two years effectively, then approximately two years terribly before his assassination.

questions.lessonContent: Emperor Diocletian implemented significant administrative reforms to address the chaos that had gripped Rome following the death of Marcus Aurelius. Diocletian was the first emperor in 100 years to properly restore order and end the violence that had plagued the empire. His administration involved increasing the bureaucracy for more effective management of the vast territory. In 285 CE, Diocletian divided the empire into two administrative realms, creating the Eastern and Western halves. This division represented the first step in the creation of what would eventually become two separate empires—the Roman (Western) Empire and the Byzantine (Eastern) Empire.
questions.question: Who divided the Roman Empire into eastern and western administrative realms?
questions.explanation: Diocletian divided the empire into two administrative realms (east and west) in 285 CE, marking the first step toward creating separate Western and Eastern empires.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Decline, Fall, and Lasting Legacy
questions.lessonTitle: Diocletian's Division of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Diocletian believed that dividing the empire for administrative purposes would strengthen the empire. In 285 CE, he divided the empire into two administrative realms—east and west. This was the first step in the creation of what would become two separate empires: the Roman (Western) Empire and the Byzantine (Eastern) Empire. Once Constantine set up Constantinople as a capital city, the east/west split deepened significantly. Diocletian was the first emperor in 100 years to properly restore order and end the violence that had plagued Rome for a century following the death of Marcus Aurelius.
questions.question: Who divided the Roman Empire into two administrative realms, and in what year?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Decline, Fall, and Lasting Legacy
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Constantine had a mother named Helena who had converted to Christianity. In 313 CE, Constantine issued the Edict of Milan, which legalized Christianity and established religious toleration throughout the empire. According to tradition, Constantine converted to Christianity on his deathbed. After Constantine's conversion, future Roman emperors were Christians. As the Western Roman Empire fell apart, the city of Rome became the headquarters of the Roman Catholic Church, with the Pope using the imperial title "Pontiff."
questions.question: Constantine issued the Edict of Milan in 313 CE, which legalized Christianity.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Decline, Fall, and Lasting Legacy
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Justinian ruled the Byzantine Empire from 527 to 565 CE from Constantinople. He married Theodora, an intelligent courtesan who became a powerful co-ruler. Justinian managed to reunite the Eastern and Western empires for a time, though this reunification did not last. His most significant accomplishment was rewriting Roman law into what became known as the Corpus Juris Civilis, or the Justinian Code, which is still the basis for civil law in several countries today. The Plague of Justinian (541-542 CE) was a bubonic plague that severely hurt the Byzantine empire, but Justinian himself recovered, though recovery for the empire took hundreds of years.
questions.question: Which of the following was an accomplishment of Emperor Justinian?
choices: Rewrote Roman law into the Corpus Juris Civilis (Justinian Code)
questions.explanation: Justinian rewrote Roman law into the Corpus Juris Civilis (Justinian Code), which is still the basis for civil law in several countries today. Constantinople was founded by Constantine, the Pax Romana began under Augustus, and the Twelve Tables were created in 450 BCE.

results.file: How we built our multi-agent research system _ Anthropic.pdf

questions.lessonContent: A multi-agent system consists of multiple agents, defined as LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop, working together to accomplish complex tasks. The Research feature involves an agent that plans a research process based on user queries and then uses tools to create parallel agents that search for information simultaneously. These systems introduce new challenges in agent coordination, evaluation, and reliability compared to single-agent systems. The architecture uses an orchestrator-worker pattern where a lead agent coordinates the entire process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. This design allows for decomposition of complex queries into subtasks that different subagents can execute simultaneously.
questions.question: What is the architectural pattern used in Anthropic's Research multi-agent system?

questions.lessonContent: In our system, the lead agent decomposes queries into subtasks and describes them to subagents, with each subagent needing an objective, an output format, guidance on the tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries. We introduced two kinds of parallelization: (1) the lead agent spins up 3-5 subagents in parallel rather than serially; (2) the subagents use 3+ tools in parallel. These changes cut research time by up to 90% for complex queries, allowing Research to do more work in minutes instead of hours while covering more information than other systems. The lead agent executes subagents synchronously, waiting for each set of subagents to complete before proceeding, which simplifies coordination but creates bottlenecks in information flow between agents.
questions.question: Early agents in Anthropic's system made errors like spawning 50 subagents for simple queries, scouring the web for nonexistent sources, and distracting each other with excessive updates. True or False: This was primarily addressed through changes to the underlying model architecture rather than prompt engineering.

questions.lessonTitle: Token Usage and Performance in Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: Our internal evaluations show that multi-agent research systems excel especially for breadth-first queries that involve pursuing multiple independent directions simultaneously. We found that a multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on our internal research eval. In our analysis, three factors explained 95% of the performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation: token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance, with the number of tool calls and the model choice as the two other explanatory factors. However, these architectures burn through tokens fast - agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats.
questions.question: The performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation is primarily explained by which single factor?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance in the BrowseComp evaluation, making it the primary explanatory factor. The three factors mentioned are token usage, number of tool calls, and model choice.

questions.moduleTitle: Prompt Engineering and Evaluation for Agents
questions.lessonTitle: Effort Scaling Guidelines for Research Agents
questions.lessonContent: Anthropic embedded explicit scaling rules in their prompts to help the lead agent allocate resources efficiently. Simple fact-finding tasks require just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls, direct comparisons might need 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each, and complex research might use more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities. These guidelines prevent overinvestment in simple queries, which was a common failure mode in early versions of their system. Without such scaling rules, agents struggle to judge appropriate effort for different tasks.
questions.question: According to the scaling rules embedded in Anthropic's prompts, how many subagents with clearly divided responsibilities are recommended for complex research tasks?

questions.moduleTitle: Prompt Engineering and Evaluation for Agents
questions.lessonContent: Anthropic used LLM-as-judge evaluation to scale the assessment of research outputs, which are difficult to evaluate programmatically since they are free-form text and rarely have a single correct answer. Their LLM judge evaluated outputs against criteria in a rubric including factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, and tool efficiency. They found that a single LLM call with a prompt outputting scores from 0.0-1.0 and a pass-fail grade was the most consistent and aligned with human judgments. This method was especially effective when eval test cases had clear answers.
questions.question: True or False: Anthropic found that using multiple LLM judges to evaluate each component of research outputs was more effective than using a single LLM call.

questions.moduleTitle: Prompt Engineering and Evaluation for Agents
questions.lessonContent: Anthropic provided their agents with explicit heuristics for tool selection because agent-tool interfaces are as critical as human-computer interfaces. They gave agents guidance to examine all available tools first, match tool usage to user intent, search the web for broad external exploration, and prefer specialized tools over generic ones. Bad tool descriptions can send agents down completely wrong paths, so each tool needs a distinct purpose and a clear description. They also found that the Claude 4 models can be excellent prompt engineers and created a tool-testing agent that rewrote flawed MCP tool descriptions.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed as an explicit heuristic Anthropic gave their agents for tool selection?
choices: Match tool usage to user intent
Prefer generic tools over specialized ones for broader coverage
Prefer specialized tools over generic ones
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states agents should 'prefer specialized tools over generic ones,' making 'Prefer generic tools over specialized ones for broader coverage' the incorrect option.

questions.moduleTitle: Prompt Engineering and Evaluation for Agents
questions.lessonContent: The evaluation process for multi-agent systems follows a specific sequence. Engineers begin by testing with small samples of around 20 queries representing real usage patterns, which allows them to spot dramatic impacts from changes in early development when effect sizes are large. Once initial testing confirms improvements, they scale the evaluation using LLM-as-judge, which evaluates outputs against criteria like factual accuracy, citation accuracy, and completeness. Finally, human evaluation is performed to catch edge cases that automation misses, such as hallucinated answers on unusual queries or subtle source selection biases.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the multi-stage agent evaluation workflow for research agents?

questions.lessonTitle: Agent Error Recovery and Stateful Execution
questions.lessonContent: In agentic systems, minor changes cascade into large behavioral changes, making it remarkably difficult to write code for complex agents that must maintain state in a long-running process. Agents can run for long periods of time, maintaining state across many tool calls, which means errors compound and we need to durably execute code and handle errors along the way. Without effective mitigations, minor system failures can be catastrophic for agents. When errors occur, we cannot simply restart from the beginning because restarts are expensive and frustrating for users. Instead, Anthropic built systems that can resume from where the agent was when the errors occurred, letting the agent know when a tool is failing and allowing it to adapt. They combine the adaptability of AI agents built on Claude with deterministic safeguards like retry logic and regular checkpoints.
questions.question: What two components does Anthropic combine to handle errors gracefully in their agent systems?
questions.answer: Retry logic and regular checkpoints (deterministic safeguards) combined with the adaptability of AI agents built on Claude

questions.lessonContent: Agent systems are highly stateful webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously. This means that whenever Anthropic deploys updates, agents might be anywhere in their process. They therefore need to prevent well-meaning code changes from breaking existing agents. Updating every agent to the new version simultaneously is not feasible because it would disrupt running agents. Instead, Anthropic uses rainbow deployments to avoid disrupting running agents, by gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously.
questions.question: True or False: Rainbow deployments allow both old and new versions of agents to run simultaneously during the transition.

questions.lessonContent: Agents make dynamic decisions and are non-deterministic between runs, even with identical prompts. This makes debugging harder because users would report agents not finding obvious information, but engineers could not see whether agents were using bad search queries, choosing poor sources, or hitting tool failures. To diagnose why agents failed and fix issues systematically, Anthropic added full production tracing beyond standard observability. They monitor agent decision patterns and interaction structures without monitoring the contents of individual conversations, to maintain user privacy. This high-level observability helped them diagnose root causes, discover unexpected behaviors, and fix common failures.
questions.question: What three specific aspects were difficult to determine when debugging agent failures before adding full production tracing?
choices: Whether agents were following the correct prompt, the correct process, or the correct trajectory
Whether agents were using bad search queries, choosing poor sources, or hitting tool failures
Whether agents were receiving correct context, generating correct outputs, or calling correct tools
Whether agents were using too many tokens, too many subagents, or too many tool calls
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that without full production tracing, engineers could not determine if agents were using bad search queries, choosing poor sources, or hitting tool failures.

questions.lessonContent: When deploying updates to agent systems, Anthropic uses a careful coordination process due to the stateful nature of agents that run almost continuously. First, they check the current agent state to understand where agents are in their processes. Then they initiate a rainbow deployment to avoid disrupting running agents by keeping both old and new versions operational. During this period, traffic is gradually shifted from the old to new versions while both versions continue running. Finally, once all traffic has been successfully migrated, the migration is complete.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the rainbow deployment process for production agent systems?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 used Kimi K2.5 as its base model for continued pretraining. This is a Mixture-of-Experts model with specific parameter configurations. The model has a total of 1.04 trillion parameters and operates with 32 billion active parameters. This base model was selected through internal evaluations measuring internal codebase perplexity, coding knowledge via FreshBench, and state tracking capabilities. The selection process also considered inference performance considerations to ensure the model would work efficiently in production.
questions.question: What are the total parameter count and active parameter count of the Kimi K2.5 base model used for Composer 2?
questions.answer: 1.04 trillion total parameters and 32 billion active parameters

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2's continued pretraining stage is divided into three distinct phases. First, the bulk of compute is spent at a 32k token sequence length to build foundational coding knowledge. Second, there is a shorter long-context extension phase that expands the sequence length to 256k tokens. Third, there is a short supervised fine-tuning phase that focuses on targeted coding tasks. This staged approach allows the model to progressively develop stronger coding capabilities before moving to reinforcement learning.
questions.question: The three phases of continued pretraining in Composer 2 are: (1) bulk compute at 32k token sequence length, (2) long-context extension to 256k tokens, and (3) a short SFT phase on targeted coding tasks.

questions.lessonContent: The Composer 2 team evaluated several potential base models before selecting Kimi K2.5, including GLM-5 and DeepSeek V3.2. They used three specific benchmarks to evaluate coding knowledge and capabilities: FreshBench for factual coding knowledge assessment, an internal state tracking benchmark similar to LoCoDiff for evaluating long-term memory during file editing, and codebase perplexity measured on their private monorepo. Kimi K2.5 achieved 83.2% on FreshBench, a state tracking score of 86, and a negative log-likelihood of 13.81M on their internal codebase. While DeepSeek V3.2 had a lower negative log-likelihood (11.75M), Kimi K2.5 was selected due to its general strong performance across all metrics and additional considerations like infrastructure efficiency.
questions.question: Which of the following benchmark results correctly matches Kimi K2.5's performance in the base model evaluation?
questions.explanation: According to Table 2 in the source content, Kimi K2.5 achieved 83.2% on FreshBench, a state tracking score of 86, and a negative log-likelihood of 13.81M. These are the exact values used in the base model selection process.

questions.lessonTitle: CursorBench Structural Differences from Public Benchmarks
questions.lessonContent: CursorBench is an internal evaluation suite comprising tasks drawn from actual coding sessions, which completely avoids train-set contamination. Compared to public benchmarks like SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual, CursorBench tasks require substantially more extensive code modifications with a median of 181 lines changed versus only 7-10 lines for public benchmarks. Additionally, CursorBench prompts are more under-specified with a median description length of only 390 characters versus 1,185-3,055 characters for public benchmarks. This combination of broad execution scope and high intent ambiguity reflects the intrinsic difficulty of real-world software engineering.
questions.question: What is the median number of lines changed in CursorBench tasks compared to SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual?

questions.lessonTitle: KL Divergence Regularization in RL Training
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses a Kullback-Leibler divergence for regularization during reinforcement learning, defined as KL(q||p) = Ex~q[-log r(x)] where r(x) = p(x)/q(x). Many open-source implementations use the k3 estimator defined as (r -1) - log r, which is an unbiased estimator that reduces variance when p and q are close. However, the technical report notes that the variance of this estimate increases drastically as p and q diverge, particularly for large KL values. Therefore, Composer 2 uses the standard k1 estimator instead, which is defined as -log r and does not suffer from variance blow-up despite being slightly biased.
questions.question: Composer 2 uses the k1 estimator (-log r) for KL divergence regularization instead of the k3 estimator. This is because the k3 estimator has a variance issue that becomes particularly problematic when the KL divergence between the policies is large.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is trained by reinforcement learning on a large set of coding tasks run in environments that emulate real Cursor sessions. The training task distribution reflects the most common use cases and captures many aspects of software engineering absent from popular AI coding benchmarks. According to Figure 3 in the technical report, the RL training tasks include the following categories: Iterate On Feature, Debugging, New Feature, Refactor, Understanding Codebase, Documentation, Testing, Code Review, Optimize, Devops, Migration, Deletion, and Other. In later stages of training, simple heuristics such as number of turns and thinking tokens of rollouts are used to upsample increasingly harder data points.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed as an RL training task category in the Composer 2 technical report?
questions.explanation: Database Design is not listed as an RL training task category. The actual categories include Debugging, Testing, and Devops (which is listed as Devops in the technical report).

questions.lessonContent: In Composer 2's RL training, the process begins with sampling a problem from our training distribution, then simulating a group of rollouts from the agent with different solutions, and finally updating the model weights based on solution quality. This creates a continuous improvement loop where the agent learns from its successes and failures in the coding environment.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the reinforcement learning training loop for Composer 2?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses Context Parallelism (CP) as the primary long-context scaling axis instead of Tensor Parallelism (TP). CP requires less communication than TP and improves compute efficiency by preserving full hidden dimensions in various projections, while TP produces less efficient skinny local matrix multiplications. To implement CP efficiently in the Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) architecture, the system computes local KV latent vectors, all-gathers the latent vectors across CP ranks, and then computes the KV projections. During continued pretraining, Composer 2 uses EP=8 and CP=2, while during RL training, it uses EP=8 and CP=8.
questions.question: What are the Expert Parallelism (EP) and Context Parallelism (CP) degrees used during the RL training phase in Composer 2?

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 achieves 61.3% on CursorBench, representing a 37% relative improvement over Composer 1.5 (which achieved 44.2%) and a 61% improvement over Composer 1 (which achieved 38.0%). The model demonstrates accuracy competitive with the strongest frontier models while being significantly cheaper at inference. According to the results table, Composer 2 achieves this performance with a Pareto-optimal trade-off between accuracy and inference cost.
questions.question: Composer 2 achieves 61.3% on CursorBench. What is the absolute percentage point improvement compared to Composer 1.5?

questions.lessonContent: The RL infrastructure for Composer 2 consists of four decoupled services: training, environments, inference, and evaluations. A decoupled service stack enables larger-scale global training, high availability, and independent scaling and sharding. The production training job for Composer 2 spanned 3 regions for GPU compute and 4 regions for CPU compute. Training uses a fully asynchronous, high-throughput training stack built on Ray and PyTorch, with a centralized reconciler performing slot-based sample lifecycle state management.
questions.question: How many regions did the production training job for Composer 2 span for GPU compute and CPU compute respectively?
questions.answer: 3 regions for GPU compute and 4 regions for CPU compute

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Setting Up Your Development Environment
questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. It serves as an ideal place for documenting common bash commands, core files and utility functions, code style guidelines, testing instructions, repository etiquette such as branch naming and merge vs. rebase, developer environment setup, and any unexpected behaviors or warnings particular to the project. There is no required format for CLAUDE.md files, but they should be kept concise and human-readable. You can place CLAUDE.md files in several locations: the root of your repo, any parent or child of the directory where you run claude, and your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md.
questions.question: What is the purpose of a CLAUDE.md file?
questions.answer: To document commands, code style, testing instructions, and project-specific information that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Setting Up Your Development Environment
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code supports placing CLAUDE.md files in multiple locations to suit different project structures. You can place a CLAUDE.md file in the root of your repo (the most common usage), where it should be named CLAUDE.md and checked into git so it can be shared across sessions and with your team. Alternatively, you can name it CLAUDE.local.md and .gitignore it. You can also place CLAUDE.md files in any parent of the directory where you run claude, which is most useful for monorepos, or in any child of the directory where you run claude, where it will be pulled in on demand when working with files in those directories.
questions.question: CLAUDE.md files can be placed in any parent directory of where you run claude and will be automatically pulled into context.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Setting Up Your Development Environment
questions.lessonContent: By default, Claude Code requests permission for any action that might modify your system, including file writes, many bash commands, and MCP tools. This deliberately conservative approach prioritizes safety. You can customize the allowlist to permit additional tools that you know are safe, or to allow potentially unsafe tools that are easy to undo. There are four ways to manage allowed tools: select "Always allow" when prompted during a session, use the /permissions command after starting Claude Code to add or remove tools from the allowlist, manually edit your .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json, or use the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions.
questions.question: Which of the following is a valid way to manage Claude's allowed tools?
choices: Using the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions
Using the /env configuration command to set tool permissions
Using the /permissions command after starting Claude Code
questions.explanation: The /permissions command, manual editing of settings files, and the --allowedTools flag are all valid methods mentioned in the content. The /env command is not mentioned as a way to manage allowed tools.

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code functions as both an MCP server and client, allowing it to connect to any number of MCP servers to access their tools. When connecting to MCP servers, there are three distinct ways to configure them: in project config (available when running Claude Code in that specific directory), in global config (available in all projects), or in a checked-in .mcp.json file which makes the MCP servers available to anyone working in your codebase. For example, you can add Puppeteer and Sentry servers to your .mcp.json, so that every engineer working on your repo can use these tools out of the box without additional setup.
questions.question: In what three ways can Claude Code connect to MCP servers to access their tools?
questions.answer: In project config, in global config, or in a checked-in .mcp.json file

questions.lessonContent: For repeated workflows such as debugging loops or log analysis, you can store prompt templates in Markdown files within the .claude/commands folder, making them available through the slash commands menu when you type /. Custom slash commands can include the special keyword $ARGUMENTS to pass parameters from command invocation. For example, putting content into .claude/commands/fix-github-issue.md makes it available as the /project:fix-github-issue command, allowing you to use /project:fix-github-issue 1234 to have Claude fix issue #1234. These commands can be checked into git to make them available for the rest of your team, and personal commands can be added to ~/.claude/commands for sessions across all projects.
questions.question: Custom slash commands can include the special keyword $ARGUMENTS to pass parameters from command invocation.

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code provides multiple ways to give Claude additional tools beyond its default capabilities. Claude inherits your bash environment, giving it access to all your standard tools, but it won't know about custom bash tools without explicit instructions on the tool name with usage examples. Additionally, Claude can leverage more complex tools through MCP servers and REST APIs. You can also create custom slash commands for repeated workflows by storing prompt templates in Markdown files within the .claude/commands folder.
questions.question: Which of the following is a method for extending Claude's capabilities?
choices: Configuring Claude's allowed tools through environment variables only
Limiting Claude's context window size in the global settings
Providing Claude with custom bash tools by telling it the tool name with usage examples
Restricting Claude's file access permissions in the project config
questions.explanation: The correct answer is providing custom bash tools, as explicitly stated in the content: 'While Claude knows common utilities like unix tools and gh, it won't know about your custom bash tools without instructions: 1. Tell Claude the tool name with usage examples'

questions.lessonContent: When following the test-driven development workflow with Claude Code, you first ask Claude to write tests based on expected input/output pairs, making it explicit that you're doing TDD so it avoids creating mock implementations. Then you tell Claude to run the tests and confirm they fail, explicitly instructing it not to write any implementation code at this stage. Finally, you ask Claude to commit the tests when you're satisfied with them before moving on to writing code.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the test-driven development workflow for writing and verifying tests?

questions.lessonContent: Beyond standalone usage, some of the most powerful applications involve running multiple Claude instances in parallel. One effective approach is to have one Claude write code while another reviews or tests it. Similarly, you can have one Claude write tests and another Claude write code to make the tests pass. You can even have your Claude instances communicate with each other by giving them separate working scratchpads and telling them which one to write to and which one to read from. This separation often yields better results than having a single Claude handle everything.
questions.question: What is a benefit of having separate Claude instances for writing code versus reviewing or testing it?
questions.answer: Having separate context often yields better results than a single Claude handling everything

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code includes headless mode for non-interactive contexts like CI, pre-commit hooks, build scripts, and automation. Use the -p flag with a prompt to enable headless mode, and --output-format stream-json for streaming JSON output. Headless mode can power automations triggered by GitHub events, such as when a new issue is created in your repository.
questions.question: Claude Code headless mode persists between sessions and does not need to be triggered each time.

questions.lessonContent: Git worktrees allow you to check out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories. Each worktree has its own working directory with isolated files, while sharing the same Git history and reflog. Using git worktrees enables you to run multiple Claude sessions simultaneously on different parts of your project, each focused on its own independent task. For instance, you might have one Claude refactoring your authentication system while another builds a completely unrelated data visualization component.
questions.question: Which of the following best describes how git worktrees function with Claude Code?
choices: Each worktree has isolated files but shares Git history with the main repository
Worktrees cannot be used with Claude Code for parallel sessions
Worktrees create completely separate Git histories for each branch
Each worktree requires its own Git repository clone
questions.explanation: Git worktrees provide isolated working directories while sharing the same Git history and reflog, allowing multiple Claude sessions to work on different tasks simultaneously.

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint is a platform for generating text embeddings, which provide a measure of the similarity or relatedness of given text queries. This endpoint was released to offer higher accuracy, longer context capabilities, and lower costs compared to other platforms. The service offers 8 open source embedding models, including top models from the MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark) leaderboard such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models. Additionally, the newly released M2-BERT retrieval models support long context lengths of 2k, 8k, and 32k tokens. The endpoint is priced up to 4x cheaper than other popular platforms, making it a cost-effective solution for various embedding needs.
questions.question: How many leading embedding models are available through the Together Embeddings endpoint?

questions.lessonTitle: Long Context Capabilities of M2-Retrieval Models
questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint includes state-of-the-art M2-Retrieval models designed specifically for long context retrieval tasks. These models significantly outperform other closed models in long context retrieval, allowing users to generate embeddings for long documents without splitting them into many short chunks. The M2-BERT retrieval models are available in three context length variants: 2k, 8k, and 32k, providing flexibility for different use cases. This means users can contain more meaningful contexts in the embeddings, resulting in better retrieval accuracy for lengthy documents. The ability to handle up to 32k context length distinguishes these models from many other embedding solutions in the market.
questions.question: The M2-Retrieval models available through the Together Embeddings endpoint support context lengths up to 32k tokens.

questions.lessonTitle: Use Cases and Applications of Embeddings
questions.lessonContent: Text embeddings generated through the Together Embeddings endpoint serve multiple purposes in AI applications. They provide a measure of similarity or relatedness between text queries, making them essential for various applications including clustering, semantic search, and classification tasks. One of the most significant use cases is Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG), which aims to overcome limitations of generative AI models by finding relevant information from a knowledge base through embeddings and providing it to a generative model. The endpoint integrates with popular vector databases such as MongoDB, Pinecone, and Chroma, as well as frameworks like LangChain and LlamaIndex, enabling developers to build comprehensive RAG systems.
questions.question: Which of the following is mentioned as a popular use case for embeddings in the content?
choices: Training large language models from scratch
questions.explanation: The content explicitly mentions that one of the most popular use cases of embeddings models is building a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system, which finds relevant information from a knowledge base through embeddings and provides it to a generative model.

questions.lessonTitle: Ordering Steps in Together Embeddings Visualization
questions.lessonContent: To visualize embedding data using the Together Embeddings endpoint, you must first define the Generate Embeddings Function to create embeddings from text inputs using the API. Next, you define the tSNE Transform Function to reduce the high-dimensional embedding vectors to 2D for visualization. Finally, you define the Plot Embeddings Function to display the transformed embeddings in a scatter plot. This sequence is essential because embeddings must be generated before they can be transformed, and transformations must complete before plotting.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in visualizing data with Together Embeddings?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint provides full OpenAI API compatibility, allowing developers who have already built applications following the OpenAI API to easily switch over. To migrate, you need to import the OpenAI client and specify your Together API key along with the base URL endpoint. The base URL must be set to "https://api.together.xyz/api/v1/embeddings" when configuring the client. Additionally, you must specify the Together model string when creating embeddings, such as "togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-32k-retrieval". This migration approach allows existing OpenAI-based applications to work with Together's embedding models with minimal code changes.
questions.question: What is the base URL required to configure the OpenAI client for the Together Embeddings endpoint?

questions.lessonTitle: Model Configuration in Together Embeddings API
questions.lessonContent: When using the Together Embeddings endpoint with OpenAI-compatible API calls, you must explicitly specify the model using Together's model API string format. The model string for the 8K context M2-BERT retrieval model is "togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-8k-retrieval". The embeddings.create method accepts this model string as a parameter and returns embedding vectors for the input text. For the 32K context version, the model string is "togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-32k-retrieval". The API returns an object where the embedding can be accessed via .data[0].embedding.
questions.question: The model parameter in the Together Embeddings API can use any OpenAI model name interchangeably with Together model strings.

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint supports integration with popular vector databases and frameworks for building Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) systems. The content explicitly mentions three vector database options that work with the Together API: MongoDB, Pinecone, and Chroma. Additionally, two framework options are mentioned for building RAG: LangChain and LlamaIndex. These integrations allow developers to store embeddings in vector databases and use them for semantic search and retrieval applications.
questions.question: Which of the following vector databases is explicitly mentioned as compatible with the Together Embeddings endpoint for building RAG systems?
questions.explanation: MongoDB is explicitly listed in the source content as one of the vector databases that can be used with Together Embeddings for building RAG systems, alongside Pinecone and Chroma.

questions.lessonContent: To generate embeddings using the Together Embeddings endpoint, you first need to initialize an OpenAI-compatible client with your API credentials. Then, you define a get_embedding function that takes text input and sends it to the API. Finally, when you call this function with text, it creates the embedding and returns the vector. This process allows existing OpenAI applications to easily switch to Together's more cost-effective embedding models.

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Systems and Data Visualization
questions.lessonContent: The M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model produces embedding vectors with 768 dimensions. However, this high-dimensional space makes direct visualization challenging, so the code uses tSNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding) to transform the embeddings into a lower-dimensional space suitable for plotting. In the provided example, tSNE is configured with 2 components for creating a 2D scatter plot visualization. The visualization code also defines a color palette using specific colors including red, blue, green, orange, and purple to distinguish between different data sources. The example processes data from multiple sources including arxiv, book, c4, and github datasets.

The code example demonstrates that texts from each data source cluster together in the visualization, showing similarities between github and stackexchange, and between book and c4.

results.file: How does image compression work_ _ Lee Robinson.pdf

questions.lessonContent: Images look smooth and continuous, but zoom in far enough and you'll see they're made of tiny colored squares called pixels. Each pixel contains three numbers indicating how much red, green, and blue to mix together, with each value ranging from 0 (none) to 255 (maximum). For example, the color rgb(255, 147, 41) represents an orange shade. An HD screenshot with 1920 × 1080 pixels contains over 2 million pixels, and since each pixel needs 3 bytes (one for R, G, and B), that's approximately 6.2 megabytes for a single image. This raw data size is why compression is necessary.
questions.question: How many color values does each pixel contain, and what is the range of each value?
questions.answer: Three values (red, green, blue), each ranging from 0 to 255

questions.lessonTitle: The Two Fundamental Approaches to Compression
questions.lessonContent: Compressing data is a core part of how computers work and powers the internet, file systems, and most software we use daily. There are two approaches to image compression. The first approach throws away the parts humans won't notice, which is called lossy compression. The second approach involves being clever about how you store every pixel, which is called lossless compression. These two ideas power JPEG, PNG, ZIP files, web traffic, and most of the internet. Without compression, the internet as we know it couldn't exist.
questions.question: The two approaches to compression are lossy (throwing away data) and lossless (being clever about storing every pixel).

questions.lessonContent: To understand why compression is essential, consider the mathematics of uncompressed image data. An HD image with dimensions 1920 × 1080 pixels contains exactly 2,073,600 pixels. Since each pixel requires 3 bytes to store its red, green, and blue components, the total raw data equals 2,073,600 × 3 bytes, which equals 6,220,800 bytes or approximately 6.2 megabytes for a single image. This substantial file size demonstrates why compression techniques are necessary to make images more manageable for storage and transmission.
questions.question: What is the uncompressed file size of a 1920 × 1080 pixel image?
questions.explanation: With 1920 × 1080 = 2,073,600 pixels, and each pixel needing 3 bytes (one for R, G, B), the calculation is 2,073,600 × 3 = 6,220,800 bytes, which equals approximately 6.2 MB.

questions.lessonContent: The PNG compression pipeline uses three key techniques in sequence. First, Filter Pixels applies prediction methods to store differences between adjacent pixels rather than raw values. After filtering, the LZ77 Pattern Find algorithm scans for repeated sequences and replaces them with compact back-references to previously seen data. Finally, Huffman Encode assigns shorter binary codes to frequently occurring values, significantly reducing the overall bit count. This specific sequence—filtering, then pattern matching, then entropy coding—forms the core of lossless PNG compression.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the PNG lossless compression pipeline?

questions.lessonContent: JPEG compression divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components. Low frequencies represent smooth gradients in the image, while high frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges. Since photographs are mostly smooth gradients, most of the information ends up in just a few low-frequency components. JPEG then throws away the high-frequency details that human eyes won't miss, keeping the smooth parts intact. This block-based transformation is what allows JPEG to achieve such dramatic file size reductions.
questions.question: What is the size of the pixel blocks that JPEG divides an image into for compression?

questions.lessonContent: Lossy compression exploits how human vision works to throw away data that won't be noticed. Your eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together, so you notice blurry edges but won't notice if colors are slightly off. JPEG converts pixels from RGB to a format that separates brightness from color, then reduces color resolution since human eyes won't notice. The tradeoff is that with lossy compression, you cannot get the original pixels back once the data is thrown away.
questions.question: With lossy compression like JPEG, can you recover the exact original pixel data after compression?

questions.lessonContent: When JPEG compression is applied at high quality settings, the difference from the original is barely noticeable to the human eye. However, when you crank up the compression ratio to achieve smaller file sizes, blocking artifacts become visible where fine details are lost. These artifacts appear as visible square blocks in areas where the high-frequency detail was discarded. This is why heavily compressed JPEG images show a characteristic blocky appearance in detailed areas.
questions.question: What type of visual artifact becomes visible when JPEG compression is cranked up to very high levels?
choices: Blurring of all colors throughout the image
Random color noise appearing in solid areas
Blocking artifacts (visible square blocks where details are lost)
questions.explanation: When JPEG compression is pushed to high levels, it discards high-frequency details from 8×8 pixel blocks, causing visible square blocking artifacts where fine details were lost. This is the characteristic distortion seen in heavily compressed JPEG images.

questions.lessonTitle: PNG Prediction Methods for Lossless Compression
questions.lessonContent: Lossless compression in PNG uses prediction to shrink file sizes. Adjacent pixels are usually similar - in a blue sky, pixels might be 128, 130, 132, 134... all close to each other. Instead of storing each value directly, PNG stores how much each pixel differs from its neighbor. PNG supports four prediction methods: Sub (predict from left neighbor, best for horizontal gradients), Up (predict from the pixel above, best for vertical gradients), Average (predict from the average of left and above), and Paeth (smartly picks between left, above, or diagonal). PNG encoders try each method per row and pick the one that compresses best.
questions.question: Which PNG prediction method intelligently chooses between left, above, or diagonal pixels to make the best prediction?

questions.lessonTitle: PNG Chunk Structure and Error Detection
questions.lessonContent: All compressed data in PNG gets wrapped in a structured format organized into chunks, each with a specific purpose. The file begins with a signature (89 50 4E 47 0D 0A 1A 0A), followed by required chunks including IHDR (Image Header with metadata like width, height, bit depth, and color type), IDAT (the actual compressed image data), and IEND (end marker). PNG files include checksums to detect corruption from issues like bad network connections or buggy programs. Each chunk includes a mathematical fingerprint called a CRC-32 checksum. When you open a PNG, your computer recalculates this fingerprint - if it doesn't match, the file is damaged.
questions.question: PNG files include checksums that act as mathematical fingerprints to detect if a file has been damaged or corrupted.

questions.lessonTitle: LZ77 Pattern Matching in PNG Compression
questions.lessonContent: After prediction filtering, PNG data may contain repeated patterns like 0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 2, 0, 0, 0, 2... The LZ77 algorithm spots these patterns and replaces them with back-references. Instead of storing the same sequence twice, LZ77 says "go back 5 values and copy 5." This tiny reference is much smaller than repeating the values. LZ77 maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data, and any pattern within that window can be referenced instead of repeated. This technique is particularly effective for images with lots of similar regions like solid backgrounds or gradients.
questions.question: The LZ77 algorithm maintains a sliding window of how much recent data when finding patterns to reference?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states 'LZ77 maintains a sliding window of the last 32 KB of data.'
